__data__.text: The Vanara women, overcome with grief, consoled and helped Tara, Vali's wife, who was deeply distraught by her husband's death.  With Sugriva's assistance, Angada, Vali's son, tearfully placed his father's body upon the funeral pyre.  Following tradition, Angada performed the cremation rites and circled the pyre before his father's spirit embarked on its final journey.  The Vanaras then proceeded to the Tungabhadra River to perform the customary water offering for the deceased. Led by Sugriva and Tara, with Angada at the forefront, they offered water to Vali's departed spirit.  Sugriva remained mournful throughout, and Rama, sharing in his sorrow, ensured the proper completion of the funeral rites.  After the cremation of the renowned Vali, Sugriva approached Rama and Lakshmana.

__data__.text:
Sugriva, overcome with grief after Vali's cremation, was surrounded by his chief advisors.  They approached Rama, who stood ready for action.  Hanuman, radiant and strong, spoke to Rama, requesting him to enter Kiskindha, the monkey kingdom, so that the newly appointed king, Sugriva, could formally install him and perform the customary rituals. Hanuman urged Rama to unite the monkeys under his leadership.

Rama, ever respectful of his father's decree, declined Hanuman's request. He explained that he was bound by a vow not to enter any village or city for fourteen years. He instructed Sugriva to formally assume the throne of Kiskindha and appoint Angada, Vali's noble and capable son, as Prince Regent.  Observing that the monsoon season had begun, Rama declared it an unsuitable time for the search for Sita. He told Sugriva to return to Kiskindha while he and Lakshmana would remain in the mountains.

__data__.text: Rama advised Sugriva to appoint Angada, Vali's eldest son, as Prince Regent, highlighting Angada's strength, valor, and noble character as befitting his position.  Noting the onset of the monsoon season, Rama declared it unsuitable for searching for Sita. He instructed Sugriva to return to Kiskindha while he and Lakshmana would remain in a comfortable mountain cave. Rama promised to help Sugriva defeat Ravana after the monsoon ended, in the month of Kartika.  Sugriva, following Rama's instructions, returned to Kiskindha and was greeted with great ceremony.  The monkeys celebrated his arrival and formally installed him as their king with traditional rituals, offerings, and honors.

__data__.text: Sugriva, following Rama's advice, entered Kiskindha, the city formerly ruled by Vali.  He was greeted by thousands of monkeys who saluted and prostrated themselves before their new king.  Sugriva graciously acknowledged his subjects and then proceeded to his brother's palace.  Emerging from the palace, Sugriva was formally installed as king with a ceremonial bath.  He received various symbolic offerings including a white canopy, golden whisks, jewels, herbs, flowers, white clothing, fragrant ointments, sandalwood, grains, honey, ghee, tiger skin, and shoes. Sixteen maidservants presented him with cosmetic pastes.  After Brahmins were honored with gifts, Sugriva was bathed with water collected from rivers, sacred sites, and seas, poured from golden pitchers and bull horns. This ritual was performed by prominent monkeys, including Hanuman and Jambavan.  Upon Sugriva's coronation, the monkeys roared with joy.  Following Rama's instructions, Sugriva then appointed Angada as Prince Regent, an act which was met with further approval from the assembled monkeys.

__data__.text: Sugriva's coronation ceremony was elaborate and steeped in tradition.  He was seated on a magnificent throne, adorned with garlands, in a beautifully decorated attic.  Water collected from various rivers, sacred sites, and even the seas was poured over him from golden pitchers and bull horns, a ritual performed by prominent monkeys like Hanuman and Jambavan, in accordance with ancient scriptures. The joyous monkeys roared their approval as Sugriva was officially crowned.  Following Rama's instructions, Sugriva then appointed Angada as Prince Regent, a decision that was met with further cheers and accolades.  The city of Kiskindha, nestled within a mountain cave, was bustling with happy, well-fed citizens and adorned with festive banners and flags, celebrating the new reign.  Having informed Rama of his coronation and the retrieval of his wife, Ruma, Sugriva, now a powerful ruler, secured his kingdom, much like Indra, king of the gods.

__data__.text: Rama and Lakshmana, having settled Sugriva into his kingship, journeyed to Mount Prasravana. They found a spacious cave ideal for their stay during the monsoon season. The mountain was alive with the sounds of wildlife – tigers, deer, roaring lions, monkeys, bears, and the calls of peacocks.  It was covered in lush vegetation, trees, shrubs, and colorful climbers, and rich in minerals.  Close by, a pond, soon to be swollen with the rains, held the promise of full-blown lotuses.  The cave, facing northeast and elevated to the west, promised shelter from the easterly winds and rains. Its entrance was marked by a smooth, black, expansive rock. To the north, a dark, imposing peak rose like a cloud, while to the south, another peak, white and gleaming, stood like a summit of the sacred Mount Kailasa.

__data__.text: Rama and Lakshmana surveyed their surroundings, finding the cave well-suited to their needs. Its northeast-facing entrance, elevated western side, and the smooth, black rock at its mouth offered protection from the monsoon winds and rain.  To the north, a dark peak loomed like a pile of kohl, while to the south, a gleaming white peak resembled Mount Kailasa.  Beyond the cave, a pristine, eastward-flowing river, reminiscent of the Mandakini, was bordered by fragrant sandalwood, Tilaka, Sal, Tamala, Atimukta, Padmaka, Sarala, and Asoka trees.  Further embellished by Vanira, Timida, Bakula, Ketaka, Hintala, Tinisha, Nipa, and Krtamala trees, the river appeared like a beautifully adorned woman.  The air was filled with birdsong, the calls of chakravaka geese, and the sight of swans and cranes.  Blue, red, and white lilies dotted the water's surface. The river, lively with ducks, peacocks, and cranes, was a peaceful haven for ascetics. Rows of sandalwood and Arjuna trees completed the picturesque scene. Rama, delighted with this idyllic location, suggested to Lakshmana that they make this their home for the monsoon season. He also noted that Sugriva's kingdom of Kiskindha was nearby, from which they could hear the joyful sounds of music and celebrating monkeys.

__data__.text: Rama and Lakshmana settled into the Prasravana hill, appreciating the beauty of the sandalwood and Arjuna trees.  Rama, finding the location ideal, proposed they stay there for the monsoon season, pointing out the proximity of Sugriva's kingdom, Kiskindha.  Sounds of celebration and music drifted from the monkey kingdom, indicating Sugriva's joy at being reunited with his wife, kingdom, and fortune. Despite the pleasant surroundings and abundant resources, Rama found no solace. The memory of his kidnapped wife, Sita, weighed heavily on him, preventing sleep and causing him constant grief, especially under the full moon. Lakshmana, sharing his brother's sorrow, urged Rama to abandon his despair. He reminded Rama of his duty, piety, and strength, emphasizing that grief would only hinder his ability to defeat Ravana. Lakshmana encouraged Rama to resolve his sorrow and focus his determination on avenging Sita's abduction, assuring him of his capability to defeat Ravana and his entire army once the monsoon season ended.

__data__.text: Lakshmana continued to counsel Rama, asserting that inaction would prevent him from defeating the cunning Ravana. He urged Rama to cast off his grief and strengthen his resolve, reminding him of his power to conquer even the earth itself, let alone Ravana.  Lakshmana advised patience until the end of the monsoon season, after which they could attack. He likened his encouragement to rekindling a fire with well-timed offerings.  Rama praised Lakshmana's devoted and wise counsel, declaring that he had cast off his grief and would renew his focus. He agreed to wait for autumn, honoring his commitment to Sugriva and acknowledging the practicality of clear rivers for their journey.  Rama affirmed the importance of repaying kindness, highlighting the hurt caused by ingratitude.  Lakshmana, pleased with Rama's renewed resolve, concurred and assured him that Sugriva would fulfill his promise. He advised Rama to patiently endure the remaining four months of the monsoon season in the lion-inhabited Prasravana hill, despite his readiness for battle.

__data__.text: Lakshmana advised Rama to control his anger and wait for the autumn season, enduring the remaining four months of the monsoon in his company. He suggested they stay on the mountain, home to many lions, even though Rama was capable of defeating Ravana immediately.

__data__.text: Having defeated Vali and placed Sugriva on the throne, Rama, now residing on Mount Malyavan, addresses Lakshmana. He notes the arrival of the monsoon season, a time previously agreed upon to pause their search for Sita. The sky is filled with massive, mountain-like clouds.  Rama describes the sky as giving birth to rain, having absorbed the ocean's water through the sun's rays. He imagines ascending the clouds to adorn the sun with garlands of Kutaja and Arjuna flowers.  The sky, patched with white clouds tinged with the red glow of twilight, resembles bandaged wounds. With gentle winds as sighs and ashen clouds like a pale face, the sky appears lovesick.  Rama compares the earth, first scorched by the sun and now drenched in rain, to Sita, shedding tears in her grief.  He describes the cool, fragrant wind, carrying the scent of Ketaka flowers, as something one could almost hold in their hands. Mount Prasravana, with its blossoming Arjuna trees, refreshed by rain, reminds Rama of the newly crowned Sugriva, free from his brother's tyranny. The mountains, cloaked in dark clouds and adorned with streams of rain, resemble students beginning their Vedic studies. The sky, illuminated by lightning and echoing with thunder, seems to groan in anguish.  Rama sees Sita's suffering reflected in the lightning flashing within the dark clouds. He observes that the obscured sky, hidden by clouds, offers solace to those separated from their loved ones.  He points out the Kutaja trees, some withered, some revived by the rain, and finds their mixed state mirroring his own conflicting emotions of grief and rekindled love. Finally, Rama notes the positive changes brought by the monsoon: settled dust, cool breezes, and the end of oppressive heat. With military campaigns halted, travelers are returning home.

__data__.text: Rama explains to Lakshmana his reasons for patiently waiting.  Observing the treacherous roads rendered impassable by the monsoon rains, Rama deemed it unwise to press Sugriva for assistance in the search for Sita, even though the monkey king was eager to help.  Furthermore, Sugriva had only recently been reunited with his wife after a long period of hardship and conflict.  Rama, understanding Sugriva's situation, felt it inappropriate to burden him immediately with his own considerable task.  He is confident that, once rested and aware of the approaching opportune time, Sugriva will remember his promise and offer his help without prompting.  Thus, Rama waits for both the end of the monsoon season and Sugriva's willing support. He adds a general observation that a noble person always remembers and reciprocates kindness, while failing to do so hurts those who have offered help. Lakshmana, after considering Rama's words, concurs, assuring him that Sugriva will indeed fulfill his promise, urging Rama to endure the temporary delay imposed by the rains while remaining focused on Ravana's eventual defeat.

in many ways at the thought of Sita, his agony of separation from her
having been accentuated by the sight of the autumnal full moon and the
water-lilies opening their petals during the night, His heart being
captured by the wealth of beauties of autumn, Sri Rama extols
the autumnal season and seeing Sugriva inactive even during
this season, sends Laksmana to whip the latter into activity

__data__.text: Rama, deeply grieved, instructs Lakshmana to deliver a stern message to Sugriva. He implores Sugriva to remember his promise and uphold the eternal virtue of keeping one's word.  He warns Sugriva not to meet the same fate as his brother Vali, who was slain by Rama and now resides in the realm of the dead.  Witnessing Rama's escalating anguish and anger, Lakshmana hardens his resolve to confront Sugriva.

__data__.text: Lakshmana, deeply concerned for his grieving brother Rama, deems Sugriva unworthy of his kingdom due to his perceived ingratitude and inaction in the search for Sita.  He declares his intention to kill Sugriva and install Vali's son as king, who would then lead the search.  However, Rama counsels Lakshmana against such rash action, urging him to approach Sugriva with diplomacy and remind him of their agreement and the urgency of the situation.  Following Rama's instruction, Lakshmana sets out for Kiskindha, his anger palpable.  His forceful journey is marked by displays of strength, uprooting trees and shattering rocks as he travels.

__data__.text: Lakshmana, fueled by anger and concern for Rama, swiftly journeyed to Kiskindha.  He moved with such force that trees were uprooted, rocks shattered, and mountains trembled in his wake.  Upon reaching the monkey city, he observed it heavily fortified and teeming with monkeys.  His anger visibly evident, he was met by the fearful stares of the monkeys outside the city.  The monkeys, in turn, armed themselves with rocks and trees upon seeing Lakshmana's approach.  Their fear quickly turned to a show of force as they prepared to defend their city.  Some were immensely strong, possessing the might of many elephants.  Lakshmana, undeterred and further enraged by their hostile display, surveyed the now inaccessible city, surrounded by the armed monkeys.  The monkeys then emerged from the city's fortifications, ready for confrontation.

__data__.text: Lakshmana, enraged, stood before Kiskindha, which was heavily guarded by fearsome monkeys armed with trees and rocks. Some monkeys possessed immense strength, comparable to that of many elephants.  The monkeys, initially taking defensive positions within the city's fortifications, emerged and openly confronted Lakshmana. Lakshmana, further angered by this show of force and Sugriva’s perceived disregard for Rama’s plight, burned with fury. His anger was palpable, like a fire shrouded in smoke. He resembled a five-headed serpent, his bow and arrow its coils and venomous fangs. Prince Angada, overcome with fear at Lakshmana's wrathful presence, approached him. Lakshmana then instructed Angada to inform Sugriva of his arrival and Rama's distress. Angada relayed Lakshmana's message to Sugriva, but the monkey king, lost in slumber and intoxicated, remained oblivious.  The other monkeys, terrified by Lakshmana's fury, raised a clamor in an attempt to appease him.

__data__.text: Angada, shaken by Lakshmana's harsh words, slipped away and sought refuge with Sugriva, Ruma, and Tara. He pleaded with Sugriva, conveying Lakshmana's message, but the king, lost in drunken slumber, remained unresponsive. The monkeys, witnessing Lakshmana's fury, raised a cacophony of alarms.  This clamor finally roused Sugriva. Disoriented and adorned only with garlands, he was approached by his advisors, Plaksa and Prabhava, who had accompanied Angada. They urged Sugriva to appease Lakshmana, reminding him of his debt to Rama and Lakshmana, who had helped him regain his kingdom. They described Lakshmana's formidable presence at the gates, his anger evident, and the monkeys' fear.  They emphasized the urgency of the situation, imploring Sugriva to meet Lakshmana with his son and kinsmen and pacify him, honoring his agreement with Rama.

Angada, fearful of Lakshmana's wrath, relayed the message to Sugriva, who was still intoxicated. __data__.text: Sugriva, upon hearing Angada's report of Lakshmana's anger, rose from his bed. He questioned his advisors, acknowledging Rama's greatness and his own lapse in judgment. Sugriva wondered why Lakshmana was angry, suspecting his enemies had spread false rumors about him.  He proposed carefully investigating the cause of Lakshmana's anger, expressing concern that even a friend's unjustified anger creates apprehension.  Sugriva emphasized the fragility of friendship and his inability to repay Rama's kindness. Hanuman then addressed Sugriva and the council, stating it was understandable Sugriva hadn't forgotten Rama's help in defeating Vali. Hanuman asserted Rama sent Lakshmana out of concern for Sugriva, reminding him that autumn had arrived, a suitable time for action, and that Lakshmana's arrival served as a reminder of Sugriva's promise to search for Sita.

He reminds Sugriva that Rama sent Lakshmana out of affection and concern, not anger.  Hanuman points out the arrival of autumn, the ideal time for the promised search for Sita. He highlights the clear skies and the inviting atmosphere, further underscoring Sugriva's delay. Hanuman advises Sugriva to tolerate any perceived harshness from Rama and Lakshmana, given their current distress. He urges Sugriva to appease Lakshmana, recognizing his own failure to fulfill his promise.  Hanuman stresses the importance of heeding counsel and reminds Sugriva of Rama's power, capable of subduing even gods and demons. He advises Sugriva to humbly submit to Rama's will, acknowledging his past debt and emphasizing the immeasurable might of both Rama and Lakshmana.

__data__.text: Laksmana, following Rama's instructions, entered the magnificent city of Kiskindha.  The monkey guards, though imposing in size and strength, respectfully greeted him. However, noticing Laksmana's anger, they kept their distance. Laksmana observed the opulent city: a beautiful cave adorned with jewels, blossoming groves, mansions, palaces, and temples.  It was fragrant with sandalwood, aloes, lotuses, and various wines.  The city boasted impressive structures, reminiscent of the Vindhya and Meru mountains, and clear streams flowed through it. He also saw the homes of prominent monkey leaders, including Angada, Hanuman, Jambavan, and Nila, located along the main road. These residences were grand, well-stocked with riches and provisions, and decorated with flowers.  Finally, Laksmana saw Sugriva's palace, a fortress-like structure enclosed by a white mountain, comparable to Indra's celestial abode.

__data__.text: Laksmana surveyed the grand homes of notable monkey leaders like Angada, Hanuman, and Jambavan, situated along the main road. These residences were opulent, filled with provisions and treasures, and decorated with fragrant flowers. He then observed Sugriva's magnificent palace, a fortress-like structure surrounded by a white, crystalline mountain, comparable to Indra's celestial abode.  The palace had white pinnacles resembling Mount Kailasa's peaks and was adorned with blossoming trees bearing desirable fruits.  Graceful trees provided cool shade. The white palace, decorated with heavenly wreaths and with gold doorways, was guarded by armed monkeys. Laksmana entered the palace unimpeded.  He passed through seven chambers filled with various furnishings before arriving at the well-guarded gynaeceum.  Inside, he saw numerous gold and silver couches with rich coverlets. He heard sweet music featuring songs accompanied by stringed instruments. Laksmana observed many women of different appearances, adorned with flowers, creating garlands, and wearing exquisite jewelry. He also noted Sugriva's attendants, who were always dedicated to their master and adorned.  Hearing the sounds of the women's anklets and ornaments, Laksmana, respectful of his vow to avoid the presence of other men's wives, felt uneasy.  Angered by the perceived neglect of Rama's situation, and the sounds from within, he loudly twanged his bowstring.

Tara then invites Laksmana inside, assuring him that his virtuous conduct is recognized and appreciated.

__data__.text: Sugriva, startled by Lakshmana's sudden, angry entrance, rose from his golden throne.  Lakshmana, deeply distressed by Rama's grief over Sita's disappearance, radiated fury. Sugriva, richly adorned, sprang to his feet, followed by his wives led by Ruma, like stars appearing after the rising of a full moon.  Sugriva, his eyes red, approached Lakshmana with folded hands. Lakshmana, unmoved, stood firm like a towering tree.  He rebuked Sugriva for his ingratitude and broken promise, reminding him of the qualities of a righteous king and the gravity of betraying a friend's trust.  He quoted a sacred verse emphasizing the heinous nature of ingratitude, for which there is no atonement.  Lakshmana condemned Sugriva's behavior, accusing him of being ignoble, ungrateful, and a liar for indulging in pleasures while failing to search for Sita, despite Rama's prior assistance in regaining his kingdom.  He insisted that Sugriva owed Rama a debt of gratitude and must prioritize finding Sita.  Lakshmana scornfully compared Sugriva to a serpent masking its voice to sound like a frog, highlighting the deceptive nature of his inaction.

He asserts that while there's atonement for various sins, there's none for ingratitude.  He accuses Sugriva of being dishonorable, ungrateful, and deceitful, having forgotten Rama's help in regaining his kingdom. Lakshmana emphasizes Sugriva's obligation to reciprocate Rama's kindness by searching for Sita.  He criticizes Sugriva's indulgence in pleasures while Rama grieves, comparing him to a serpent disguising its voice.  Lakshmana reminds Sugriva that he owes his kingship to Rama's compassion and warns him of dire consequences, similar to Vali's fate, if he continues to disregard his duty.  He concludes by observing that Sugriva's obliviousness to Rama's power and the potential repercussions is the reason for his careless pursuit of pleasure while neglecting Rama's urgent need.

__data__.text: Tara, addressing the enraged Lakshmana, urged him to speak kindly to Sugriva.  She emphasized that Sugriva, the king of monkeys, did not deserve harsh words, especially from Lakshmana. Tara defended Sugriva, stating he was neither ungrateful nor deceitful, nor cruel.  She reminded Lakshmana that Sugriva had not forgotten Rama's help in regaining his kingdom, wife Ruma, and Tara herself. Tara compared Sugriva's lapse in attention to that of Sage Viswamitra, who, engrossed in celestial pleasures, lost track of time. She pleaded with Lakshmana to forgive Sugriva's momentary lapse, emphasizing that even the wise can succumb to exhaustion and distraction. Tara urged Lakshmana to control his anger and seek the truth before reacting.  She reminded him that thoughtful individuals like Lakshmana should not give in to rash anger.  Tara interceded for Sugriva, asking Lakshmana to quell his rage.  She expressed her belief that Sugriva valued Rama's friendship above all else – even his wives, kingdom, and possessions. Finally, Tara expressed confidence that Sugriva would reunite Rama with Sita after defeating Ravana, and she noted the vast number of ogres present in Lanka.

__data__.text: Tara continued her plea to Lakshmana, emphasizing Sugriva's loyalty to Rama. She asserted that Sugriva would gladly give up everything—his wife Ruma, Tara herself, his son Angada, his kingdom, wealth, and even livestock—to please Rama.  Tara was certain Sugriva would reunite Rama with Sita after defeating the wicked Ravana, just as the moon god is reunited with his consort Rohini. She described the immense ogre army in Lanka, numbering hundreds of thousands of crores.  Tara explained that defeating Ravana required first overcoming this formidable army of shape-shifting ogres.  She reminded Lakshmana that even Sugriva couldn't achieve this alone, unaided. Recalling Vali's words, Tara revealed the vastness of Ravana's forces.  She explained that Sugriva had sent messengers to gather a massive monkey army from all directions for assistance, and he was awaiting their arrival before marching on Lanka.  Tara urged Lakshmana to be patient, assuring him that the monkey reinforcements, including bears and baboons, would arrive that very day.  Finally, she implored Lakshmana to calm his anger, noting the fear and anxiety it caused among the monkey wives, who were still traumatized by Vali's death.

He orders vast numbers of powerful monkeys to mobilize immediately, likened to storm clouds filling the sky.  These swift messengers are to locate and bring back all monkeys from across the land.  Hanuman obeys Sugriva's command, dispatching the monkey messengers to all directions.  These monkeys quickly ascended into the sky, traveling along the paths of birds and celestial bodies. They sought out monkeys inhabiting various terrains – seashores, mountains, forests, and lakesides – urging them to join the cause of Rama and travel to Kishkinda. Fearful of Sugriva's wrath, the monkeys swiftly complied.  Three crores of exceptionally strong monkeys departed from the Ajana mountain.  Ten crores more, the color of molten gold, mobilized from the western mountain where the sun sets. Thousands of crores, radiating like a lion's mane, descended from Mount Kailasa.  Millions more, sustained by fruits and roots, came from the Himalayas. Thousands of crores of formidable, reddish monkeys journeyed from the Vindhya range.  Countless others, residing near the Milk Ocean, in Tamalavana forest, and along riverbanks, also joined the ranks. This massive monkey army advanced, seemingly eclipsing the sun.  The messengers sent to hasten the already departing monkeys reached the Himalayas and spotted a giant tree in Lord Shiva's sacred grounds.

__data__.text: The monkeys descending from the Vindhya range were a fearsome sight, reddish in color and known for their formidable deeds.  Meanwhile, countless others emerged from various locations – the shores of the Milk Ocean, the Tamalavana forest, and along riverbanks.  Their numbers were too vast to count.  This enormous army of monkeys advanced, their multitude seemingly obscuring the sun.  The messengers dispatched to rally the monkeys reached the Himalayas and discovered a massive tree in a sacred area associated with Lord Shiva.  This area was revered as the site of a past sacrificial ceremony, conducted to honor Lord Shiva, which brought joy to all the gods.  Miraculously, the remains of the offerings had produced fruits and roots with a taste akin to ambrosia.  Anyone who consumed these sacred provisions would feel satiated for a month.  The monkeys, naturally sustained by fruits, collected these special provisions, along with celestial herbs, to bring back to Kishkinda.  They even gathered fragrant flowers from the sacred ground as a gesture of goodwill towards Sugriva.  Having spurred all the monkeys on earth to gather, the messengers swiftly returned with the news to Kishkinda, arriving at the very hour they had departed.  Presenting the collected herbs, fruits, and roots to Sugriva, they announced, “We have searched all the mountains, rivers, and forests; every monkey on earth is heeding your command and making their way here." Sugriva, overjoyed at this report, graciously accepted the offerings.

__data__.text: Sugriva, having received gifts from his monkey subjects and dismissed them, felt that his and Rama's purpose was nearly fulfilled. Lakshmana politely suggested they leave Kishkindha, and Sugriva readily agreed. After dismissing Tara and the other women, Sugriva summoned his closest advisors and ordered his palanquin.  He and Lakshmana then rode in the gold palanquin, accompanied by a large, armed escort, to the place where Rama was staying. Upon arriving, Sugriva and Lakshmana approached Rama with folded hands, prompting the other monkeys to do the same.  Pleased by this display of respect, Rama lifted Sugriva from where he had prostrated himself and embraced him warmly, inviting him to sit. Rama then advised Sugriva on kingship, emphasizing the importance of balancing dharma (righteous conduct), artha (economic prosperity), and kama (pleasure). He stressed that neglecting dharma and artha for kama leads to downfall.  Sugriva expressed his gratitude to Rama and Lakshmana for helping him regain his kingdom and his honor.  He then informed Rama that hundreds of monkey chiefs had assembled, having gathered all the powerful monkeys from across the world.

They both ascended the gleaming gold palanquin, carried by numerous monkeys.  Under a white canopy, with white whisks waving around him, Sugriva, now experiencing true kingship, was celebrated with conches, drums, and the praises of bards.  Surrounded by hundreds of armed monkey warriors, he journeyed to where Rama was staying. Upon reaching the blessed location, the radiant Sugriva and Lakshmana dismounted and approached Rama with respectful, folded hands.  Observing Sugriva's gesture, the other monkeys followed suit, creating a scene that pleased Rama.  He gently lifted Sugriva from his prostrate position and embraced him warmly. He then proudly reported the impressive assembly of monkey chiefs and their forces – hundreds, thousands, millions, and even greater numbers – from all corners of the earth, ready to serve Rama. These powerful monkeys, Sugriva explained, are comparable to Indra himself, resembling clouds and mountains in their might, dwelling in the grand mountains of Meru and Vindhya.  They eagerly await Rama's command to battle Ravana and retrieve Sita.

Leaping, growling, and swarming, they surrounded Sugriva like clouds around the sun.  The strongest monkeys, calling out loudly, bowed their heads to Sugriva from afar, seemingly hesitant to push through the dense crowd. Some monkey chiefs approached Sugriva with formal reports and then departed. Others met with Sugriva and remained respectfully by his side.  Sugriva quickly informed Rama of the arriving monkeys’ desire to settle and rest. Then, standing respectfully with folded hands before Rama, Sugriva addressed the monkey chiefs, instructing them to strategically position their forces near mountain streams and throughout the forests.  He emphasized the importance of a skilled general assessing the strength and number of these troops.

__data__.text: Sugriva instructs Vinata, a powerful monkey general, to lead a search party of one hundred thousand monkeys eastward. Their mission is to locate Sita and Ravana's dwelling.  The search area encompasses a vast region including mountains, forests, and riverbanks, specifically naming the Bhagirathi (Ganga), Sarayu, Kausiki (Kosi), Yamuna, Saraswati, Sindhu (Indus), and Sona rivers, along with the Mahi and Kalamahi regions.  Furthermore, they are to explore various territories including Brahmamala, Videha, Malawa, Kasi, Kosala, Magadha, Pundra, Anga, regions known for silk production and silver mines.  Sugriva also directs them to search Yavadwipa (Java), including its seven kingdoms and islands rich in gold and silver, and a mountain called Sigira.  He further specifies the search should extend to the  swiftly flowing Sona river, mountain streams, and forests, particularly noting areas where large demons are said to dwell.  The search party is ordered to continue to the sea inhabited by Siddhas and Caranas, then to a reddish sea called the Red Sea, where they may find a giant Salmali tree.

__data__.text: Sugriva directs Vinata's search party towards a series of islands and oceans. First, the terrifying Iksudwipa islands within the roaring Iksusamudra ocean, where large, perpetually hungry demons snatch flying creatures with their shadows. Next, they must cross the loud, serpent-infested ocean to the Red Sea, where they will find the giant Kutasalmali tree and Garuda's jeweled abode. On an island within a wine-like ocean, mountain-like ogres called Mandehas hang upside down, falling into the water at sunrise, scorched by the sun and slain by holy incantations, only to revive and reattach themselves. Beyond lies the Ksiroda, the ocean of milk, with its pearly white waves, in the middle of which rises the white Mount Rsabha with its fragrant, blossoming trees. Atop Mount Rsabha, they will find the Sudargana lake, resplendent with gold-filamented lotuses and frequented by divine beings. Crossing the Ksiroda leads to an ocean that terrifies all beings, containing the immense Vadavamukha, a submarine fire born of a sage's wrath.  A golden palmyra tree marks the eastern boundary of this ocean, beyond which lies the golden Mount Uday, the source of the sunrise.  Its vast, sky-high summit forms a base for other mountains.  Adorned with golden trees, Mount Uday features the peak Saumanasa, where Vishnu once placed his foot during his cosmic strides.  The sun is most visible from Jambudwipa when ascending this peak. Before Mount Uday shines the island of Sudarsana, bringing light to all beings. Sugriva commands the search party to thoroughly examine this mountain's peaks, caves, and forests for Ravana and Sita. The eastern horizon glows red, illuminated by the brilliance of the golden mountain and the sun.

Atop the western mountain stands a magnificent palace complex, built by Viswakarma,  filled with palaces and lush trees teeming with birds. This is the abode of Varuna. Between Mount Meru and the western mountain stands a giant, ten-branched golden palmyra tree. Sugriva instructs the monkeys to search all these locations – the difficult-to-access lakes, the rivers, and the mountains – for Sita and Ravana. Continuing beyond Kala mountain, Satabali is to search Sudarsana mountain, and then Devasakha, a haven for birds. He is to explore its thickets, waterfalls, and caves.  Sugriva then describes a vast, desolate expanse devoid of life, which Satabali must cross to reach Mount Kailasa, home to Kubera's magnificent palace.  He is to search the moonlit slopes and caves of Kailasa. Finally, Sugriva instructs him to cautiously explore the difficult-to-access cave of Kraufica mountain, inhabited by radiant sages, and to investigate its other caves, plateaus, peaks, caverns, and slopes as well.

__data__.text: Sugriva continues his meticulous instructions to Satabali, directing him to search the moonlit caves and slopes of a mountain for Ravana and Sita.  He cautions Satabali about the Kraufica mountain, advising vigilance while entering its difficult-to-access cave, inhabited by radiant, god-like sages. Sugriva emphasizes a thorough search of the surrounding caves, plateaus, peaks, and slopes of Kraufica. He then mentions the Manasa peak, a desolate place devoid of life, including gods, demons, and even birds.  Continuing, Sugriva instructs Satabali to explore Mainaka mountain, home to Maya's abode, and the surrounding area inhabited by Kinnara women.  He then directs Satabali to a hermitage of perfected ascetics of the Vaikhanasa and Valakhilya orders, suggesting a respectful inquiry about Sita.  Nearby, lies a golden lotus-covered Vaikhanasa lake, frequented by Kubera's elephant, Sarvabhauma. Beyond the lake stretches a vast, starless, sunless expanse, illuminated by the aura of self-realized sages.  Sugriva guides Satabali further, mentioning the Sailoda river, bordered by Kicaka bamboos, which help the sages cross.  Finally, he describes the land of the Uttara Kurus, blessed with numerous streams adorned with lotus leaves resembling cat's-eye jewels.

__data__.text: Sugriva describes a region beyond the Vaikhanasa lake, illuminated by the aura of ascetic sages.  The Sailoda river flows through this region, its banks lined with Kicaka bamboos that aid the sages in crossing.  This river marks the entrance to the land of the Uttara Kurus, a land of reward for those who have performed good deeds.  This land abounds with streams fed by lotus ponds filled with golden lotuses.  The streams themselves are rich with dark green lotus leaves, resembling cat's-eye jewels.  Lakes the color of the rising sun, adorned with red and gold lotuses, add to the beauty of the land. Blue lotuses with gem-like petals and golden filaments also thrive there. The rivers' sandy banks are scattered with pearls, precious gems, and gold, bordered by mountains of jewels and gold that shine like fire.  The trees in this land are always in bloom and laden with fruit, exuding a divine fragrance and offering delightful tastes and textures. They fulfill all desires. Some trees provide clothing of various shapes and sizes, and others offer ornaments of pearls and cat's-eye jewels suitable for both men and women.  Certain trees bear fruit enjoyable in all seasons, while others produce fruits resembling precious gems.  There are trees that offer comfortable beds with colorful covers and pleasing garlands.  Other trees provide luxurious drinks, various foods, and the company of accomplished and beautiful women.  The land is also home to Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, Nagas, and Vidyadharas, all radiant beings who enjoy life with their companions.  Everyone in this land is said to have performed good deeds in their past lives, and they now live in a state of constant joy and abundance, surrounded by wealth, luxury, and youthful companions. The air is filled with the delightful sounds of music, singing, and laughter, creating a harmonious atmosphere that pleases all.

__data__.text: Sugriva continues his description of the lands beyond the Vaikhanasa lake, detailing a land of unimaginable abundance and pleasure.  Trees miraculously provide luxurious beds with ornate covers and fragrant garlands, along with delicious food and drinks.  Even beautiful and talented companions are provided for by the magical trees of this land.  Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Siddhas, Nagas, and Vidyadharas, all radiant beings, live there, enjoying life's pleasures with their companions.  Everyone in this land is said to have earned this reward through good deeds in past lives.  Music, singing, and laughter fill the air, and no one experiences unhappiness or engages in negativity.  Goodness flourishes in this land.  Sugriva then mentions a massive golden mountain called Somagiri, located beyond this land in the Northern Sea.  Visible even from the heavens of Indra and Brahma, this mountain illuminates the surrounding region with its own brilliance.  Divine beings like Vishnu, Shiva, and Brahma reside in this area.  Sugriva warns the monkeys not to venture beyond the Uttara Kurus, as the path is impassable even for gods. He advises them to return after sighting Somagiri.  He emphasizes that the region beyond is unknown and without limits. Sugriva urges the monkeys to thoroughly search the described areas, and even beyond, with the ultimate goal of finding Sita.  He stresses that finding Sita will please Rama greatly, and even more so, himself.  He promises to reward them handsomely for their success, ensuring they will enjoy lives of comfort, peace, and companionship with their loved ones.

Rama, entrusting Hanuman with the vital task, urged him to utilize his immense strength and valor to locate Sita, the daughter of Janaka.

__data__.text: King Sugriva, the foremost of monkeys, addressed his assembled troops, urging them to thoroughly search their designated areas as instructed by him to fulfill Rama's objective.  The monkey chiefs, understanding the gravity of their mission, spread out like locusts across the land.  Meanwhile, Rama and Lakshmana remained on Mount Prasravana, awaiting news of Sita's whereabouts. Satabali hastened towards the north, Vinata towards the east, and Hanuman, accompanied by Tara and Angada, journeyed south.  Susena, a powerful warrior, headed west.  Sugriva, having dispatched his forces, felt content.  The monkey generals, roaring and shouting, marched with determination, vowing to find Sita and defeat Ravana. Some boasted of their individual strength and ability to retrieve Sita single-handedly, even from the underworld, claiming they could shatter mountains, split the earth, and churn the oceans.

Another bragged he could demolish trees, shatter mountains, split the earth, and churn the oceans.  Yet another asserted that nothing could stop him, whether on land, in the sea, in the mountains, forests, or even the depths of the underworld. They made these pronouncements in front of Sugriva.

__data__.text: Sugriva explains to Rama the source of his geographical knowledge.  He recounts how he once guarded the entrance of a cave while his brother Vali fought a demon inside. When blood filled the cave and Vali didn't emerge, Sugriva assumed the worst and sealed the cave.  He returned to Kiskindha and assumed leadership, but Vali eventually reappeared, having slain the demon.  Fearful, Sugriva relinquished his position, but Vali, enraged, chased him across the world. Sugriva describes seeing various rivers, forests, and cities as he fled, the earth appearing like a mirror and a firebrand due to his speed.  He eventually reached the eastern region, observing diverse trees, mountains, and lakes, including a mineral-rich mountain and the mythical Milk Ocean.

__data__.text: Sugriva continues his story, describing his flight from Vali.  He ran so fast that the earth seemed like a blur, reflecting everything like a mirror and appearing like a firebrand.  He ran east, observing diverse trees, mountains, lakes, and even a mountain rich with minerals and the mythical Milk Ocean, home to celestial nymphs.  He turned back and then suddenly departed for the south, passing through the Vindhyan range with its sandalwood trees.  He saw Vali pursuing him again and again and continued fleeing west, taking note of the western mountain.  He then ran north, reaching the Himalayas, Mount Meru, and even the Northern Sea, still pursued by Vali.  Finally, Hanuman reminded Sugriva of a sage's curse on Vali, forbidding him from entering a certain hermitage.  They found refuge on Mount Rsyamuka, safe from Vali due to the curse.  Sugriva emphasizes that this flight allowed him to directly observe the entire world.

__data__.text: Sugriva dispatched the foremost monkeys to search for Sita.  They thoroughly investigated lakes, riversides, lands, and cities, leaving no area unexplored. Following Sugriva's detailed instructions, the monkey leaders meticulously searched their assigned regions, including mountains, forests, and woodlands.  They searched throughout the day, gathering at night to rest. They found fruit-bearing trees in every region they explored and slept beneath them. After a month of searching, the monkey chiefs returned to Sugriva and Rama, empty-handed. Vinata, having explored the east, returned with his group.  Satabali, having searched the north, returned with his troop, fearful.  Susena, having searched the west, also returned to Sugriva. They approached Sugriva and Rama, bowing before them. They reported having searched all mountains, dense forests, rivers, and lands. They investigated every cave and bower. They searched for and eliminated large animals in difficult and uneven terrains, suspecting they might be Ravana in disguise. They emphasized that even the most inaccessible areas were searched repeatedly, yet Sita remained undiscovered.  They concluded that only Hanuman, with his noble character and lineage, was capable of finding her, as he had fortunately gone to the same region where Sita had been taken.

__data__.text: Hanuman, accompanied by Tara and Angada, journeyed to the region assigned by Sugriva.  They traveled a great distance, exploring the Vindhyan range's caves and dense forests, but found no trace of Sita.  The monkeys sustained themselves on roots and fruits, searching tirelessly through difficult terrain. This particular region was challenging, full of caves, dense forests, and desolate wilderness.  After exhausting that area, they moved on to another, equally challenging region. This new area was barren – the trees were fruitless and leafless, the rivers dry, and there were no animals to be found. The land had been cursed by the sage Kandu after the death of his young son.  It was in this cursed forest that the monkeys encountered a fearsome demon, who stood like a mountain and threatened them.

__data__.text: Entering a luminous grove within the cave, the monkeys, weary and thirsty, discovered a wondrous spectacle.  Golden trees, some resembling the rising sun and standing on gem platforms, bore vibrant blossoms and leaves.  Lotus plants of a striking blue hue added to the surreal beauty. Fruit-laden trees buzzed with golden bees, and various honeys lay nearby. __data__.text: Hanuman addressed Swayamprabha, the ascetic woman residing in the cave, explaining that his group, driven by hunger, thirst, and exhaustion, had stumbled into the darkness-shrouded cave.  Upon entering the large cavern, they were bewildered by the dazzling array of objects within, fearing it might be an illusion.  He questioned the ownership and origin of the golden trees, the food, the opulent palaces and mansions adorned with gold and gems, the fragrant blossoms, and the golden lotuses in the clear water, even wondering about the golden fish and turtles.  Hanuman implored Swayamprabha to explain these wonders to them, as they were ignorant of their nature. Swayamprabha began her explanation by revealing that a powerful magician named Maya had created the golden grove. She explained that Maya was formerly the architect of the demon chiefs and that he had created the magnificent palace through his skill and the boon he received from Brahma, which granted him the creative power and resources of Sage Sukra. Maya enjoyed this power and the grove for a time until Indra, angered by Maya's attachment to the nymph Hema, slew him.  Brahma then bestowed the grove and its luxuries upon Hema. Swayamprabha, daughter of Merusavarni, revealed that she guarded Hema's home as a favor to her friend, the skilled dancer and singer.  She then inquired about the monkeys' purpose in the grove and how they had found this hidden place, requesting they share their story after they had eaten and rested.

Maya, the architect of the demons, created this magnificent palace after performing intense austerities for thousands of years. Brahma granted him a boon equivalent to the wealth of Sage Sukra, including creative power, resources, and architectural knowledge. Maya enjoyed this power and the grove for a time until Indra, enraged by Maya's attachment to the nymph Hema, killed him. Brahma subsequently gifted the grove and its luxuries to Hema. Swayamprabha, daughter of Merusavarni, explained that she safeguards Hema's home as a favor to her friend, a skilled dancer and singer. She then questioned the monkeys' purpose for being in the grove, asking why they journeyed through such challenging terrains, and how they discovered this hidden place.  She invited them to share their full story after they had eaten and refreshed themselves.

__data__.text: Hanuman, addressing Swayamprabha, recounted their journey. After resting and enjoying the fruits offered by her, Hanuman explained their mission.  He described how Rama, the noble king, comparable to Indra and Varuna, entered the Dandaka forest with his brother Lakshmana and wife Sita.  Sita was abducted from Janasthana by Ravana. Hanuman continued, explaining they served Sugriva, a valiant monkey king and friend of Rama.  Sugriva sent them, including Angada and other leading monkeys, to the southern region protected by Yama and inhabited by Sage Agastya. Their mission: to find Ravana and Sita.  Having searched the forest and facing hunger, they found a large, dark cave concealed by vegetation.  Birds emerged from the cave, wet and covered in pollen, suggesting water within.  Hanuman encouraged the other monkeys to enter, hoping to find water. They cautiously proceeded into the darkness, holding onto each other.

__data__.text: The monkeys, emerging from the cave wet and covered in pollen, confirmed Hanuman's suspicion of water within.  He urged them to enter, a sentiment shared by the group, eager to find relief.  Driven by their thirst and the urgency of their mission, they ventured deep into the dark cave, holding onto each other.  Hanuman reminded them of their purpose: to find Sita and Ravana.  He then addressed Swayamprabha, explaining their plight.  Hungry and weary, they had gratefully accepted her hospitality. In return, they offered their services.  Swayamprabha, pleased with their visit, declined their offer, stating her virtuous life required no assistance.  Hanuman, however, pressed the matter, explaining that they had exceeded the time allotted by Sugriva for their search and were now in danger.  He pleaded with her to help them escape the cave. He further emphasized their failed mission due to their entrapment, highlighting the importance of their task.

__data__.text: Hanuman, anxious about overstaying their mission deadline, implored Swayamprabha to help them escape the cave, emphasizing the importance of their task to find Sita and Ravana.  Swayamprabha agreed to help them, using her ascetic powers.  She instructed the monkeys to close their eyes, assuring them that this was necessary for their safe passage.  The monkeys complied, covering their eyes with their hands, eager to escape.  Swayamprabha swiftly transported them out of the cave. Reassuring the monkeys, she pointed out their surroundings – the Vindhya range and the Prasravana mountain on one side and the Indian Ocean on the other – and bid them farewell before returning to the cave.

__data__.text: The monkeys discovered the vast, roaring ocean.  Their allotted month to search for Sita had expired while exploring Maya's illusory mountain fortress.  Seeing the blossoming trees near the Vindhya mountains, they realized spring had arrived, and they had failed their mission.  Angada, the prince, addressed the anxious monkeys, reminding them they had left Kiskindha in the month of Aswina under Sugriva's command, and that time had now run out.  He praised their experience, loyalty, and strength, reminding them they had placed him in charge of the expedition.  He declared that since they had failed Sugriva's mission, death was certain, and proposed fasting until death as a preferable alternative to facing Sugriva's wrath, given the monkey king's fierce temper and newfound authority.

He lamented his predicament, highlighting Sugriva's temper and his own prior conflict with the king.  The other monkeys agreed, fearing Sugriva's anger and Rama's potential indifference. They resolved to return to Sugriva only if they found Sita, otherwise, they would choose death. Tara, however, suggested returning to the well-provisioned, inaccessible cave, where they would be safe from everyone, including Sugriva, Rama, and even Indra.  Reassured by Tara and Angada, the monkeys agreed to this plan, seeking a way to avoid Sugriva's deadly punishment.

__data__.text: Hanuman, observing Angada's inclination to follow Tara's advice, perceived a potential challenge to Sugriva's rule. He saw Angada as a formidable force, intelligent, strong, and growing in influence, akin to the waxing moon.  Recognizing the need to sway Angada back to Sugriva's side, Hanuman employed his eloquence to create discord among the monkeys.  He then attempted to intimidate Angada by highlighting the fickle nature of the monkey troop and their unlikely acceptance of his leadership without their families. Hanuman emphasized his own loyalty to Sugriva, along with that of Jambavan, Nila, and Suhotra, asserting they would not be swayed by Angada, whether through persuasion or force.  He cautioned Angada against challenging a stronger opponent like Sugriva, reminding him that even the seemingly impenetrable cave they sought refuge in could be easily destroyed by Lakshmana's powerful arrows, which were capable of shattering even mountains.

Hanuman reiterated that Lakshmana's arrows would be merciless.  Finally, he offered an alternative: return with him to Sugriva, submit, and be reinstated in Kiskindha.  He painted Sugriva as a virtuous, trustworthy ruler who cared for Angada's mother and lacked other heirs, further incentivizing Angada's return.

He accuses Sugriva of taking his elder brother's wife while he was still alive, and questions Sugriva's loyalty, recalling how he sealed the cave entrance while his brother Vali fought, and later forgot Rama's kindness. He expresses distrust in Sugriva, believing he would eliminate Angada, a potential rival to the throne.  Angada, fearing imprisonment or worse, announces his decision to fast unto death rather than return to Kishkindha. He instructs the monkeys to convey his well-being to Sugriva, Rama, Lakshmana, and his mothers, Ruma and Tara, specifically asking them to comfort Tara.

__data__.text: Angada declares he will fast unto death at that very spot rather than return to Kishkindha. He instructs the monkeys to inform Sugriva, Rama, Lakshmana, and his mothers, Ruma and Tara, of his decision and well-being, emphasizing the need to comfort Tara. He predicts Tara will be devastated by the news of his death.  After speaking, Angada sits down on the sacred grass, grief-stricken. The other monkeys, weeping and lamenting, join his fast, denouncing Sugriva and praising Vali.  They formally begin their fast by sipping water, facing east on the sacred grass.  These monkeys, contemplating their imminent deaths, recall the events leading to this crisis: Rama's exile, Dasaratha's death, the havoc in Janasthana, Sita's abduction, Jatayu's death, Vali's death, and Rama's anger.  As the mountain fills with the roaring of numerous monkeys resembling mountain peaks, the caves resonate with their cries, like the sky echoing with thunder.

__data__.text: Sampati, Jatayu's brother, a powerful and long-lived vulture, emerged from a Vindhyan cave.  Seeing the monkeys gathered, he rejoiced, believing they were destined to be his long-awaited meal. He declared his intention to devour them one by one as they succumbed to starvation.  Overhearing this, a worried Angada remarked to Hanuman that this felt like a deliberate attack orchestrated by Yama, the god of death, disguised as Sampati, to thwart their search for Sita.  He lamented that Rama's mission and Sugriva's orders remained unfulfilled while a new crisis arose.  Angada praised Jatayu's selfless act of defending Sita, contrasting it with their own arduous, yet unsuccessful search.  He declared Jatayu fortunate to have died fighting Ravana, escaping the perceived tyranny of Sugriva, and achieving a blessed state. Angada concluded that the monkeys were now endangered due to Dasaratha's death, Jatayu's demise, and Sita's abduction.

__data__.text: Sampati, lamenting his hunger, declared his intention to devour the monkeys. Angada, distressed, questioned their misfortune and praised Jatayu's noble sacrifice for Rama, contrasting it with their own struggles. He attributed their current plight to Dasaratha's death, Jatayu's demise, and Sita's abduction, blaming Kaikeyi's actions for their predicament.  Overhearing Angada's lament, Sampati, intrigued and moved, inquired about the details of his brother Jatayu's death, recalling him with fondness.  Unable to fly due to his burnt wings, he requested the monkeys' assistance in descending from the mountain, expressing his eagerness to learn about Jatayu, Dasaratha, and Rama.

__data__.text: Sampati, expressing gratitude for their assistance, stated his desire to descend from the mountain peak.  He shared his joy at hearing Jatayu's praises after such a long time, describing his younger brother as virtuous and valiant.  Eager to learn more, he asked the monkey leaders about Jatayu's demise, inquiring specifically about the circumstances of his death in Janasthana.  He also inquired about the fate of King Dasaratha, a friend of Jatayu and father of Rama, whom he described as beloved and respected.  Due to his sun-scorched wings, Sampati was unable to fly and therefore requested the monkeys' help in getting down.

__data__.text: Angada, still grieving over Jatayu’s death, tried to reason with Sampati, who intended to eat the monkeys. Sampati’s words, though hoarse with sorrow, did not assuage the monkeys’ fear, as they remained suspicious of his motives.  The monkeys, already resigned to starvation, assumed Sampati would devour them. They reasoned that if they died this way, their purpose would be fulfilled, achieving a swift end.  Reaching this grim conclusion, the monkey leaders helped Sampati down from the mountain. Angada then began to narrate their story to Sampati. He spoke of his grandfather, the mighty monkey king Riksraja, and his two sons, Vali and Sugriva. He highlighted his father, Vali's, renowned strength and deeds.  Continuing his tale, Angada described how Rama, the noble son of Dasaratha and rightful king, entered the Dandaka forest with his brother Lakshmana and wife Sita, adhering to his father's wishes and the path of righteousness.  He then recounted Sita's abduction by Ravana and how Jatayu, a friend of Rama's father, witnessed the act and intervened. Despite his age and weakened state, Jatayu fought valiantly against Ravana, destroying his chariot and rescuing Sita, but ultimately perished in the battle.  Angada mourned Jatayu's death at the hands of the powerful Ravana, and how Rama performed his last rites. He further explained how Rama formed an alliance with his uncle, Sugriva, resulting in Vali’s death. After installing Sugriva as king, Rama tasked the monkeys with finding Sita. Despite their extensive search, they were unable to locate her, much like searching for sunlight in the darkness of night.

__data__.text: Angada continued his story, explaining that Rama allied with his uncle, Sugriva, and killed Vali. Sugriva, who had been previously banished by Vali, was then installed as the new king of the monkeys.  Under Rama's direction, Angada and the other monkeys searched extensively for Sita, but their efforts proved fruitless. They thoroughly explored the Dandaka forest, even venturing into a hidden cavern built by the demon Maya.  Unfortunately, their month-long search, as stipulated by Sugriva, ended without success.  Having surpassed the allotted time, the monkeys, fearing Sugriva and Rama’s anger, resigned themselves to death by starvation.  They believed that even if they returned, their lives would be forfeit.

__data__.text: Sampati, overcome with grief, revealed to the despairing monkeys that Jatayu, whom they spoke of as slain by Ravana, was his younger brother.  He lamented his inability to avenge his brother due to his old age and lack of wings.  Sampati recounted how he and Jatayu, in their youth, flew towards the sun.  Jatayu faltered near the sun's intense heat, and Sampati shielded him with his own wings, which were subsequently burnt. He fell upon the Vindhyas and lost track of his brother.  Hearing this, Angada asked Sampati if he knew Ravana’s whereabouts.  Sampati, though weakened, declared his intent to help Rama through his knowledge.  He claimed awareness of various realms and events, including conflicts between gods and demons, and pledged to assist in Rama’s quest despite his age and diminished strength.

__data__.text: Sampati, despite his weakened state, vowed to aid Rama's quest using his knowledge.  He claimed awareness of celestial events and declared his intent to help Rama through words.  He recounted seeing Ravana abducting a beautiful, jeweled woman who cried out "Rama!" repeatedly. Her silken robe contrasted sharply with Ravana's dark complexion.  Sampati deduced that this woman must be Sita.  He then revealed Ravana's location: the island city of Lanka, a hundred yojanas away, built by Vishwakarma.  He described the city's opulent architecture and Sita’s imprisonment within Ravana's palace. Sampati urged the monkeys to travel swiftly to Lanka’s southern shore, assuring them of a safe return, and explained the varying flight heights of different birds, beginning with the lowest fliers.

__data__.text: Sampati advises the monkeys to travel to Lanka's southern shore, a hundred yojanas across the sea, where they will find Ravana.  He assures them of a safe return and details the varying flight heights of different birds, from the lowest (sparrows and grain-eaters) to the highest (Garuda). He mentions vultures, his own kind, are descended from Garuda's brother, Aruna.  Sampati declares his intent to avenge his brother Jatayu's death at Ravana's hands, an act facilitated by the monkeys' journey.  He claims powerful vision, inherited from his lineage, enabling him to see Lanka and Sita. Sampati further explains that vultures can see great distances due to their diet and ancestry.  He then urges the monkeys to find a way across the sea, promising their quest will be successful. Finally, Sampati requests to be taken to the seashore to perform a ritual offering of water to his deceased brother, Jatayu.

__data__.text: Sampati, the king of vultures, relayed the information about Sita's abduction to the monkey leaders, who were relieved to hear the news.  Jambavan, the foremost of monkeys and bears, inquired about the details of Sita's abduction, including who witnessed it, who abducted her, and her current location. He questioned who would dare defy the might of Rama and Lakshmana's arrows. Sampati consoled the monkeys, who were eagerly awaiting news about Sita, and began his tale. He described how he fell on a remote mountain long ago, becoming old and frail. His son, Suparswa, cared for him by bringing him food.  One day, as Sampati was hungry, Suparswa returned empty-handed.  Suparswa explained that he had positioned himself near the Mahendra mountain to hunt for creatures from the sea. He then saw someone resembling a dark cloud carrying a woman as bright as the dawn. Suparswa intended to seize them for Sampati's meal but was asked to allow them passage.

__data__.text: Suparswa, positioned near Mahendra mountain, waited to hunt sea creatures for his father, Sampati. He spotted a figure, dark as kohl, carrying a woman radiant as the sunrise.  Intending to capture them, Suparswa was instead politely asked to let them pass. He honored the request, acknowledging the power of gentle words. The figure, radiating brilliance, swiftly departed. Afterward, airborne sages informed Suparswa that the woman was Sita and, fortunately, still alive. They also identified her abductor as Ravana. Suparswa watched the grieving Sita, stripped of her jewels and silken veil, desperately calling for Rama and Lakshmana. He relayed this news to his father, Sampati, who, despite his wingless state, felt compelled to help Rama.  Sampati expressed confidence in the monkey leaders, sent by Sugriva, highlighting their strength and wisdom. He declared that Rama's arrows, divinely crafted and fletched with buzzard feathers, possessed the power to protect or conquer the three worlds. Though Ravana was mighty, Sampati believed nothing was beyond the capabilities of the assembled monkey leaders.

__data__.text: Sampati, having performed his brother's last rites, addressed the assembled monkeys, urging them to listen attentively as he recounted how he learned of Sita's whereabouts. He described how, long ago, he fell upon the Vindhyan mountains, his wings burned by the sun.  He lay unconscious for six days, and upon waking, was disoriented.  Eventually, he recognized the landscape: the Vindhyan range by the southern sea, teeming with birds and riddled with caves.  He recalled a hermitage in that area, once home to the sage Nisakara, a place he and Jatayu had frequented. Sampati descended the mountain and made his way to the hermitage site, where fragrant breezes blew and trees overflowed with blossoms and fruit. He sought shelter under a tree, hoping to see Nisakara, and soon spotted the radiant sage returning from his bath, accompanied by a variety of animals.

__data__.text: Sampati, seeking refuge near Nisakara's hermitage, found the area lush with blossoming, fruit-laden trees and filled with sweet-smelling breezes.  He rested beneath a tree, hoping to see the sage. Soon, Nisakara appeared, radiating light, returning from his bath.  A variety of animals, including bears, deer, tigers, lions, and snakes, surrounded him like devotees around a generous benefactor. As the sage reached his hermitage, the animals dispersed to their own homes.  Nisākara, noticing Sampati, re-emerged from his dwelling and inquired about Sampati’s condition, observing his missing feathers and burned wings, and recalling a time when Sampati and his brother, Jatayu, powerful shape-shifting vultures, would visit him.  He asked Sampati to explain his injuries, whether caused by illness, accident, or some punishment.

__data__.text: Sampati recounted to the sage Nisakara his rash pursuit of the sun.  He explained his difficulty in speaking, due to injuries and shame from his earlier defeat by Indra.  He and his brother Jatayu, fueled by pride, had vowed to follow the sun to its setting point.  From the sky, they saw cities the size of chariot wheels, heard music and ornaments jingling, and observed groups of women in red clothing.  Ascending further, the forest below resembled grass, mountains looked like pebbles, and rivers appeared as threads. The Himalayas, Vindhyas, and Mount Meru looked like elephants in a pond.  Overcome by exhaustion, fear, and confusion, they fainted.  Disoriented, they struggled to regain their senses, the sun appearing as large as the earth. Jatayu then descended without warning, prompting Sampati to follow.

__data__.text: Sampati's vision faltered, his mind struggling to comprehend the overwhelming sight of the sun. With immense effort, he refocused, the sun appearing as large as the earth itself.  Jatayu suddenly descended without warning, prompting Sampati to follow.  In the descent, Sampati shielded Jatayu with his own wings, saving his brother from being burned by the sun's intense heat.  Sampati, however, was not so fortunate; his own wings were severely burned. He believed Jatayu had fallen somewhere in Janasthana while he himself landed, unconscious and injured, on the Vindhya mountains.  Devastated by the loss of his rulership, his brother, his wings, and his strength, Sampati resolved to end his life by leaping from a mountain peak.

__data__.text: Sampati recounted his woes to the sage Nisakara.  The sage comforted him, prophesying that Sampati would regain his wings, sight, strength, and vitality.  Nisakara shared a prophecy about a king named Dasaratha and his exceptionally powerful son, Rama.  Rama, along with his brother Lakshmana and wife Sita, would be exiled to the forest.  There, the demon king Ravana would abduct Sita.  Though offered delicacies, the grieving Sita would refuse all food.  Indra would send her a divine dish, but Sita would offer it to her absent husband and brother-in-law.  Monkeys, acting as Rama's messengers, would eventually find Sampati, who was instructed to tell them Sita's location. The sage advised Sampati to remain where he was, patiently awaiting the restoration of his wings. Nisakara explained that by staying, Sampati would perform a great service by helping Rama find Sita and defeat the evil Ravana, benefiting everyone, including Sampati himself.  Although eager to see Rama and Lakshmana, Nisakara expressed his desire to soon depart from his physical body.

__data__.text: Nisakara advised Sampati against leaving, assuring him that his wings would be restored in due time.  He emphasized that by staying put, Sampati would perform a vital service to humanity by aiding Rama in locating Sita and vanquishing Ravana. This act would benefit everyone, including Sampati, the princes Rama and Lakshmana, Brahmins, sages, and even Indra.  Nisakara confessed his own longing to see Rama and Lakshmana, but declared his readiness to relinquish his physical body, having already attained spiritual enlightenment.

He waited for centuries, enduring agony and doubt after Nisakara's passing.  Sampati recalls reprimanding his son Ravana for not rescuing Sita, especially given the distress it caused Rama and Lakshmana and out of respect for the late King Dasaratha.  As he spoke, Sampati's wings miraculously regrew. Overjoyed, he declared this a sign of the monkeys' success in their search. He then took flight, testing his newfound wings. Inspired by Sampati's words and the miraculous return of his wings, the monkeys continued their journey south, filled with renewed hope and determination to find Sita.

__data__.text: Upon learning Sita's location from Sampati, the jubilant monkeys, strong as lions, journeyed towards the ocean, the gateway to Ravana's kingdom.  Arriving at the northern shore of the vast Indian Ocean, they were awestruck by its immensity. The ocean seemed to shift in nature, appearing calm in some parts, turbulent in others, and elsewhere, its waters rose like mountains.  The monkeys became disheartened, fearing the ocean's depths and the creatures within.  They questioned how their mission could possibly succeed. Witnessing their despair, Angada, their leader, reassured and encouraged them, emphasizing that giving in to fear would only lead to failure.  He reminded them of the importance of courage and determination when faced with a challenge.  As night passed, Angada again conferred with the elder monkeys, surrounded by the monkey army, a force as impressive as Indra's own. He questioned who among them possessed the strength and resolve to cross the formidable ocean and help Sugriva fulfill his promise to rescue Sita.

__data__.text: Angada, surrounded by the monkey army, addressed the esteemed elders and the assembled troops. He questioned who among them possessed the strength and courage to cross the vast ocean and fulfill their promise to Sugriva by rescuing Sita. He asked who could leap across the immense distance, alleviate their fears, and allow them to return home safely to their families. Angada further inquired who would enable them to joyfully reunite with Rama, Lakshmana, and Sugriva.  He implored anyone capable of this feat to step forward and declare their ability, offering a reassuring vow to the anxious assembly.  Met with silence, Angada reiterated his plea, reminding the monkeys of their renowned strength, lineage, and honored status, urging them to reveal their leaping capabilities.

__data__.text: The monkey leaders, prompted by Angada, each declared their leaping prowess. Gaja claimed a distance of ten yojanas, Gavaksha twenty, Sarabha thirty, and Rsabha forty.  Gandhamadana boasted of fifty yojanas, Mainda sixty, Dwivida seventy, and Susena eighty.  Jambavan, respectfully acknowledging his comrades, admitted his age had diminished his former strength, yet declared he could still leap ninety yojanas. He emphasized the importance of their mission, endorsed by Sugriva and Rama, and recalled his past glory of circumambulating Lord Trivikrama during Bali's sacrifice.

__data__.text: Jambavan declared his leaping capacity to be ninety yojanas, but reminded the monkeys that his strength had diminished with age. He recounted how, in his youth, he had circumambulated Lord Trivikrama during Bali's sacrifice.  Now, however, he felt his current capability was insufficient for the task at hand, the rescue of Sita. Angada responded respectfully, offering to leap one hundred yojanas, though uncertain of his return. Jambavan, however, dissuaded Angada, arguing that a leader should not be risked on such a perilous mission.  He emphasized Angada's importance to their cause, likening him to the protected mistress of a household and the essential root of their endeavor.  Jambavan affirmed that Angada, with his wisdom and valor, was the key to Sita’s rescue and that the monkeys relied upon him for success.

Jambavan continued to emphasize Angada's importance to their mission.  He argued that Angada must be protected, like a cherished wife, because he is fundamental to their success, the very root of their endeavor.  Just as a tree thrives only when its roots are healthy, so too will their search for Sita succeed only with Angada's leadership. Jambavan reminded Angada of his wisdom and strength, declaring him the key to rescuing Sita, the one the monkeys relied upon.

Angada responded that if neither he nor any other leader stepped forward, they would be forced to fast until death.  He stressed the importance of Sugriva's command and the dire consequences of failing him.  Returning to Kishkindha without Sita would surely invite Sugriva's wrath and lead to their demise. Given these grave circumstances, Angada urged Jambavan, whose wisdom he greatly respected, to find a solution.  Jambavan reassured Angada that his purpose would not be thwarted. He declared he would appeal to someone capable of accomplishing their mission, and turned to Hanuman.

__data__.text: Jambavan continues his encouraging speech to Hanuman, recounting the story of Hanuman's birth. He describes how the wind-god became captivated by Anjana's beauty, removing her garment as she stood on a mountain peak.  He then embraced her, resulting in Hanuman's conception.  Jambavan emphasizes that Hanuman's birth was divinely ordained, with the wind-god foretelling his son's strength and intelligence. As a child, Hanuman, mistaking the rising sun for a fruit, leaped towards it, reaching an astonishing height.  His ascent was interrupted by Indra, who, angered by Hanuman's audacity, struck him with a thunderbolt, injuring his chin and giving him the name "Hanuman." The enraged wind-god then ceased his activity, causing turmoil in the three worlds until the gods, led by Brahma, pacified him.  Brahma then bestowed upon Hanuman the boon of invulnerability in battle.

He compares his passage through the sky to the Milky Way, visible to all, and declares that only Garuda or his father, the wind-god, could match his power. He envisions his leap as a lightning bolt across the sky and likens his form to Vishnu's Trivikrama form. He moved with the might of a lion, startling birds and unintentionally crushing plants and animals beneath his massive form.  Reaching the base of the mountain, vibrant with colorful minerals and frequented by mythical beings, Hanuman paused, his size dwarfing even the largest elephants. He offered respectful salutations to the gods and the natural world, steeling his resolve. Focusing his power, he grew to immense proportions, drawing the attention and admiration of his fellow monkeys. With the force of his hands and feet, he pressed down upon the mountain, causing it to tremble and release a shower of fragrant blossoms, covering the landscape in a floral blanket. The mountain, under the strain of Hanuman's incredible strength, even began to release streams of water, like an elephant in rut.

__data__.text: Hanuman's immense power continued to shake Mount Mahendra.  The pressure caused the trees to shed their blossoms, blanketing the mountainside in a fragrant, colorful layer of petals.  Water gushed forth from the mountain, much like an elephant in rut.  Streams of molten gold, silver, and antimony flowed from the mountain’s ore-rich veins. Massive boulders, some containing realgar, were dislodged and tumbled down the slopes, resembling smoke billowing from a fire.  Creatures living within the mountain sought refuge in caves, their terrified cries echoing across the land. Snakes, disturbed by the tremors, bit at the rocks, their venom causing the stones to ignite and shatter.  Even the mountain’s medicinal herbs could not neutralize the potent venom.  Ascetics, Vidyadharas, and their families, mistaking the upheaval for an attack by powerful spirits, fled the mountain in fear.  The Vidyadharas, adorned with garlands and red markings, left behind their feasts and golden vessels, clutching their swords and shields. Their wives, adorned in jewelry, joined them in the sky, watching in astonishment.  The Vidyadharas, resembling wise sages, hovered in the air, observing the chaotic scene below, demonstrating their mastery of magical flight.

They had abandoned their golden vessels, food, weapons, and ornaments in their hasty retreat.  The men, adorned with garlands and red markings, and their wives, decked in jewelry, watched from the sky as Hanuman made ready. They heard the pronouncements of the sages, celestial bards, and demigods also watching from the heavens, who declared that Hanuman, son of the wind-god, was about to attempt the impossible feat of leaping across the vast ocean to Lanka, for the sake of Rama and his monkey allies. Bracing his massive arms against the mountain, he crouched, gathering his strength and courage for the monumental leap.  Looking upwards, he took a deep breath, focusing on the daunting distance ahead.

__data__.text: Hanuman, preparing for his monumental leap across the ocean, retracted his limbs and focused his strength, courage, and energy.  He gazed upwards, assessing the vast distance to Lanka, holding his breath in anticipation.  Planting his feet firmly, he drew back his ears, ready to launch himself.  The mighty monkey, addressing his fellow simians, declared his intention to fly to Ravana's Lanka with the speed of one of Rama's arrows. He vowed to find Sita, or else continue to the heavens themselves in search of her.  Failing that, he swore to bring Ravana back in chains.  One way or another, he would return successful, with Sita, or even with all of Lanka itself.  With this pronouncement, Hanuman propelled himself into the air with immense force and speed, likening himself to the mighty Garuda. The force of his ascent uprooted trees, their branches flailing, which were carried aloft with him as he soared through the clear sky.  These airborne trees, adorned with flowers and perched-upon birds, followed Hanuman for a time, like a retinue accompanying a departing king.  The sight of the enormous monkey, surrounded by a cloud of uprooted, blossoming trees, was a wondrous spectacle.  As Hanuman continued his journey over the sea, the uprooted trees, unable to sustain their flight, plunged into the salty depths below.

__data__.text: Failing that, he swore to bring Ravana back in chains.  One way or another, he would return successful, with Sita, or even with all of Lanka itself.  With this pronouncement, Hanuman propelled himself into the air with immense force and speed, likening himself to the mighty Garuda. The force of his ascent uprooted trees, their branches flailing, which were carried aloft with him as he soared through the clear sky.  These airborne trees, adorned with flowers and perched-upon birds, followed Hanuman for a time, like a retinue accompanying a departing king.  The sight of the enormous monkey, surrounded by a cloud of uprooted, blossoming trees, was a wondrous spectacle.  As Hanuman continued his journey over the sea, the uprooted trees, unable to sustain their flight, plunged into the salty depths below.  Covered in the scattered blossoms, buds, and shoots from the falling trees, Hanuman resembled a cloud, or a mountain illuminated by fireflies.
