__data__.text: Hanuman's face, reflecting the coppery hue of his nose, glowed like the sun at dusk.  His coiled tail streamed behind him, resembling a grand banner raised in honor of Indra.  The brilliant Hanuman, with his white teeth and curled tail, shone like the sun surrounded by a halo.  His deep red rump was striking, like a mountain of red chalk split open.  The wind rushing through Hanuman's armpits as he flew over the ocean roared like thunder.  He resembled a meteor streaking across the sky, or a mighty elephant with a girth around its waist.  His reflection mirrored in the water below, Hanuman looked like a ship sailing on the sea, propelled by the wind.  The sea churned beneath him, agitated by his immense speed and power.  He crashed through towering waves, his momentum causing the ocean to roar.  He pulled huge waves in his wake as he sped forward. He continued his journey, seemingly counting the massive waves as he passed.  Water sprayed into the air by his passage mingled with clouds, creating a beautiful spectacle. Whales, crocodiles, alligators, and turtles were exposed as the water was displaced, much like limbs revealed by the removal of clothing. Serpents, witnessing Hanuman's powerful flight, mistook him for Garuda, the mythical bird.

__data__.text: Hanuman, seemingly counting the enormous waves as he flew, soared over the ocean, his immense speed causing the water to spray high into the air, mingling with the clouds. Whales, crocodiles, alligators, and turtles were briefly exposed as the water surged around him. Serpents, observing his powerful flight, mistook him for the divine bird Garuda. Hanuman's massive shadow, stretching for miles, followed him across the sea's surface.  He appeared like a winged mountain, his energy radiating as he traversed the sky. The sea below seemed to dip and curve as if forming a trough in response to his passage. He flew like Garuda, parting clouds as he went.  Clouds, white, reddish, blue, and madder-colored, trailed behind him.  He moved in and out of the cloud banks, appearing like the moon emerging from behind cover. Gods, Gandharvas, and demons showered him with flowers as he flew.  The sun did not burn him, and the wind-god provided a refreshing breeze to aid his journey.  Sages praised him, and gods and Gandharvas sang his praises.  Nagas, Yakshas, and even ogres marveled at his strength and lack of fatigue, offering him their acclaim as he continued his flight.  The ocean god, eager to honor the lineage of Ikshvaku to which Rama belonged, watched Hanuman's progress thoughtfully.

__data__.text: The sun god did not burn Hanuman, the monkey chief, as he flew across the sky on his mission for Rama. The wind god sent a cool breeze to refresh him. Sages praised Hanuman as he flew, and gods and Gandharvas sang his praises.  Nagas, Yakshas, and even Rakshasas marveled at his strength and energy.  The ocean god considered how to honor Hanuman because of Rama's lineage from the noble Ikshvaku dynasty. He reflected that failing to assist Hanuman would bring ill repute. He recalled how the Ikshvaku king Sagara had expanded his realm, and determined that Rama's aide should not face hardship. The ocean god decided that Hanuman should rest and regain strength before continuing his journey.  He then addressed Mainaka, a golden mountain submerged in the ocean, reminding him of his placement by Indra as a barrier against the demons of the netherworld.  He instructed Mainaka to rise from the water so Hanuman could rest, emphasizing the importance of assisting those associated with the Ikshvaku lineage. The ocean god urged Mainaka to fulfill this duty, lest the virtuous become angered, and promised that Hanuman would continue his journey after resting on the mountain, frequented by gods and Gandharvas.

__data__.text: The ocean god, Varuna, urged Mainaka, a golden mountain, to rise from the sea and offer Hanuman, Rama's emissary, a place to rest. Varuna stressed the importance of aiding those connected to the Ikshvaku dynasty, reminding Mainaka of how King Sagara had expanded their realm. He assured Mainaka that Hanuman would continue his journey after resting.  Mainaka obeyed, emerging from the water like the sun breaking through clouds. Its golden peaks, inhabited by mythical beings, gleamed brightly. Hanuman, mistaking the sudden appearance of the mountain for an obstacle, struck it with his chest. Recognizing Hanuman's power, Mainaka, now assuming a human form, praised Hanuman for undertaking such a difficult journey.

The mountain, Mainaka, recognized Hanuman's strength and, rather than being offended, roared in response.  Taking on a human form atop his peak, Mainaka addressed Hanuman with respect and urged him to rest.  He explained that the ocean, expanded by the ancestors of Rama, wished to honor Hanuman by offering him hospitality. Mainaka had been specifically asked by the ocean god to extend this courtesy, as Hanuman had travelled a great distance and deserved respite.  Mainaka offered Hanuman a variety of delicious fruits, roots, and bulbs, and emphasized their shared connection. He praised Hanuman as a renowned figure, full of virtues, and the greatest of all leaping monkeys, comparing him to the wind god, his father. Mainaka explained that honoring Hanuman was akin to honoring the wind god himself, further explaining that in ancient times, mountains had wings and flew like giant birds.  Their movement caused fear among the gods and other beings who worried about being crushed.

__data__.text: Mainaka, the mountain, praised Hanuman as the son of the powerful wind-god, equal to his father in speed.  He explained that honoring Hanuman also honored the wind-god.  Mainaka recounted a tale from Satyayuga, when mountains had wings and flew like giant birds. Their flight terrified the gods and other beings.  Indra, angered by the fear they caused, used his thunderbolt to cut off the mountains' wings.  Mainaka revealed that he too was targeted by Indra, but Hanuman's father, the wind-god, saved him by tossing him into the sea.  Grateful for this past kindness, Mainaka offered Hanuman hospitality, urging him to rest and enjoy the fruits of the mountain.  However, Hanuman politely declined, explaining his urgent mission to find Sita and his promise not to delay.  He touched the mountain as a gesture of respect and continued his journey skyward, observed with admiration by the spirits of both the mountain and the ocean. Leaving the mountain and ocean far behind, Hanuman soared even higher, following the path of the wind, his father.

She further informed him of a boon granted by Brahma, allowing her to devour anyone who crossed her path.  Hanuman, in response, explained his mission to find Sita, who had been kidnapped by Ravana while Rama was occupied.  He asked Surasa to assist him, as a resident of Rama's vast kingdom. He proposed that if she insisted on consuming him, he would return after fulfilling his mission to find Sita and report to Rama. Surasa, unyielding, declared that no one escapes her due to her boon. Determined to gauge Hanuman's strength, she prepared for a confrontation.

A contest of size ensued, with Hanuman growing larger and Surasa widening her mouth to match, from ten to one hundred yojanas.  Seeing this immense, gaping maw, Hanuman cleverly shrunk himself down to the size of a thumb and quickly flew in and then out of her mouth.  He then addressed Surasa, stating he had fulfilled her condition and now would continue his search for Sita. Surasa, impressed, reverted to her true form and gave Hanuman her blessing to find Sita and reunite her with Rama.

The path he traversed was a vibrant and celestial realm, frequented by various beings and adorned with stars, planets, and clouds of different hues.

He surveyed the landscape below, noting the nearing coastline, forests, and rivers as he approached Lanka. Recognizing his imposing size might attract unwanted attention, Hanuman wisely considered altering his form to avoid detection.

He also saw the surrounding sea, its coastal wetlands, the trees growing there, and the river mouths flowing into the ocean.  Aware of his own immense size, comparable to a massive cloud that seemed to fill the sky, Hanuman wisely considered that his appearance might arouse the curiosity of the island's inhabitants.  Therefore, he reduced his size back to his normal form, much like a sage regaining inner peace.  Having thus diminished his impressive stature, Hanuman, now in his usual form, reached the shores of Lanka. He then landed on a peak of Mount Lamba, rich with fruit trees and flowers, resembling a massive cloud.  From this vantage point, he surveyed Lanka situated on Mount Trikuta. __data__.text: Hanuman, having crossed the vast ocean, landed on the Trikuta mountain, where he rested.  He appeared radiant, covered in a shower of blossoms from the surrounding trees. Despite his long journey of hundreds of miles, he felt no fatigue. Confident in his ability to cover vast distances, he reflected on the relatively short distance across the sea to Lanka.  The mighty monkey then proceeded towards Lanka, passing through fragrant meadows and honey-filled groves. He continued his journey through blossoming forests and over mountains, eventually spotting Lanka perched atop a mountain peak.  From his vantage point, he observed a variety of trees in full bloom, including pines, Karnikaras, date-palms, Priyalas, orange trees, Kutajas, Ketakas, fragrant pepper trees, Kadamba trees, Saptacchadas, Asanas, Kovidaras and Karaviras.  He also saw trees laden with flowers and buds, teeming with birds and swaying in the wind. The landscape was further adorned with ponds filled with swans and ducks, covered in lotuses and water lilies, along with various pleasant gardens and diverse bodies of water, all shaded by fruit and flower-bearing trees of every kind.

__data__.text: Hanuman observed Lanka, adorned with blossoming Sarala, Karnikara, date-palms, Priyala, Muculinda, Kutaja, Ketaka, fragrant pepper trees, Kadamba, Saptacchada, Asana, Kovidara, and Karavira trees. The trees, heavy with flowers and buds, teemed with birds and swayed in the wind. Ponds filled with swans and ducks and covered with lotuses and water lilies dotted the landscape, along with various pleasant gardens and diverse bodies of water shaded by fruit and flower-bearing trees.  The magnificent city, protected by Ravana, was surrounded by moats filled with lotuses and water lilies. Guarded by ogres wielding formidable bows, the city boasted a golden wall, towering buildings like autumn clouds, white-plastered roads, hundreds of mansions decorated with flags and pennons, and stunning golden archways adorned with climbers.  Perched atop a mountain, Lanka appeared like a celestial city, seemingly floating in the air, a testament to the craftsmanship of Viswakarma.  Hanuman imagined the city as a woman, its fortifications like hips and loins, the sea and surrounding woods her garments, weaponry her hair, and mansions her earrings.  He approached the northern gate, reminiscent of Kubera's city, Alaka, and pondered the formidable task ahead. The city, teeming with fierce ogres, well-constructed and once occupied by Kubera, was now heavily guarded. Considering the city's defenses, the surrounding sea, and the power of Ravana, Hanuman contemplated the monkeys' chances of success, believing Lanka to be unconquerable even by the gods.

__data__.text: Hanuman, observing Lanka, reflected on its impenetrable defenses. The city, once Kubera's, teemed with fierce, heavily armed ogres.  Considering the city's fortifications, the surrounding ocean, and Ravana's power, Hanuman doubted even the gods could conquer it.  He questioned what Rama could do against such odds.  Hanuman saw no possibility of negotiation, bribery, or even warfare succeeding against the ogres. He believed only four monkeys, including himself, could even reach Lanka.  Hanuman's priority was Sita's safety. He resolved to discover whether she was alive before taking further action.  Pondering his next move, Hanuman realized his current form wouldn't allow him to infiltrate the heavily guarded city.  He needed to be unseen yet effective.  Hanuman sought a way to find Sita without being detected by Ravana, fearing failure would ruin Rama's mission.  He knew a careless approach could jeopardize everything.

His primary concern was Sita's safety and the success of Rama's mission. He knew any misstep could have dire consequences, and a timid approach would be as disastrous as open conflict. He questioned how he could see Sita alone and unnoticed, fearing discovery would ruin everything.  He believed even the wind couldn't move through Lanka undetected by the watchful ogres.  Recognizing the danger of his natural form, Hanuman decided to shrink himself to a smaller size under the cover of night.  He planned to enter the city unseen, searching every corner for Sita.  As the sun finally set, Hanuman, eager to begin his search, reduced himself to the size of a cat and swiftly entered the beautifully structured city of Lanka.

Its well-planned streets were lined with grand mansions, their golden pillars and ornate windows giving the city a celestial appearance.  Hanuman observed the impressive seven and eight-story buildings, adorned with crystal, gold, cat’s-eye gems, and strings of pearls.  Elegant golden archways further enhanced the city’s beauty.  The sight of this impressive city filled Hanuman with a mix of awe and apprehension. While amazed by Lanka's splendor, he also felt a renewed sense of urgency to find Sita.  As he continued his search, the moon rose, casting its bright light across the city. Hanuman paused to admire the moon, its white glow reminiscent of milk, a lotus fiber, or a shining conch shell, and its appearance like a swan gracefully gliding across a lake.

Hanuman, filled with awe, surveyed the magnificent city of Lanka.  The opulent entrances, adorned with platforms of cat’s-eye gems, diamonds, crystals, and pearls, captivated him.  Floors of gems, golden elephants, and silver vaults added to the city's splendor.  Stairways of cat’s-eye led to crystal-walled interiors, free of dust and housing elegant assembly halls. The towering structures seemed to reach the sky.  The sounds of clarionets and tinkling ornaments echoed throughout Lanka, along with the calls of herons and swans. However, reflecting on the prowess of Rama and Lakshmana, Hanuman felt reassured.

Lanka, bathed in the glow of lights and celestial bodies, appeared to Hanuman like a bejeweled woman. Its defensive walls resembled her raiment, the houses her earrings, and the armories her breasts. As Hanuman entered the city, Lanka, the presiding ogress, revealed herself in her true, monstrous form.  Seeing Hanuman, she rose up and challenged him, demanding to know his identity and purpose. She warned him that Lanka, protected by Ravana’s forces, was impenetrable. Hanuman responded by questioning the ogress’s identity and the reason for her anger. It was a paradise on earth, resplendent with jewels and flowers, resembling a pollen-covered mountain peak, illuminated by its inhabitants. It was like a magnificent aerial car, soaring through the sky, drawn by elegant swans. Within the palace, Hanuman saw an aerial car adorned with precious stones, as beautiful as a multi-hued cloud, resembling a mountain peak rich with minerals, under a sky filled with planets and the moon. The ground around the aerial car was decorated with artificial hills of gems and gold, covered with artificial trees bearing artificial flowers, complete with filaments and petals.  White mansions, pools with flowers, lotuses, groves, and lakes were also present.  Hanuman marveled at the vast aerial car, Puspaka, named after flowers, capable of long journeys, shining brightly with gems, and considered a premier residence of the gods.  Artificial birds of cat's-eye, silver, and coral, along with jewel-encrusted serpents and beautifully formed horses, were also featured. Birds with charming beaks and wings adorned with coral and gold flowers, playfully contracting their wings, resembled companions of Cupid. Within Puspaka, artificial elephants with ornate trunks, adorned with lotus filaments, offered worship to Goddess Lakshmi, whose image, holding a lotus, was also present. Hanuman was awestruck by the splendor of the aerial car, which resembled a mountain with lovely caverns, and a fragrant, blossoming tree in springtime.

__data__.text: Hanuman observed the sleeping women. Their lips were closed, their eyes shut, and a lotus-like fragrance emanated from them.  Their faces, once vibrant like open lotuses, were now closed like lotus blossoms at night. Hanuman likened the women's faces to flowers, attracting bees eager for their nectar. The chamber, illuminated by the women, resembled a starlit autumn sky.  Ravana, amidst the women, shone like the moon surrounded by stars. Hanuman thought the women resembled fallen stars, returned to the heavens.  Their beauty and radiance mirrored the brilliance of bright stars. Their hair and jewelry were disarrayed from their recent revelries, some missing earrings or necklaces, others with loosened hair and garlands.  Some women's forehead markings were smudged, anklets askew, and necklaces scattered. Others lay entangled in broken necklaces or with garments slipped, resembling exhausted mares. Some were without earrings, their garlands crushed like blossoms trampled by an elephant.  Pearl necklaces, dislodged and gleaming, resembled rays of sun and moon, or swans nestled between their breasts.  The edges of their garments, stirred by their breath, fluttered like colorful streamers.  The movement of their breath also caused their earrings to tremble gently.  The air was filled with the sweet scent of alcoholic beverages from their breath. Some women, in their drunken stupor, mistook their fellow wives' mouths for Ravana's.  Lost in their infatuation with Ravana, they inadvertently brought pleasure to one another through this confusion. Some women used their arms or garments as pillows.  They lay intertwined, limbs resting on each other, enjoying the physical contact.  Their linked arms formed a human garland, adorned by resting bees attracted to their hair and skin.

__data__.text: Hanuman continued to observe the sleeping women.  Their pearl necklaces, dislodged, lay between their breasts, shining like the sun and moon or resembling sleeping swans.  Some wore necklaces of cat’s-eye gems that looked like Kadamba birds, while others had gold chains that resembled Cakrawaka birds.  Their thighs, adorned with jewels and the lines of their bodies, appeared like riverbanks populated by swans and Cakrawaka birds.  Small bells on their girdles resembled flower buds, while larger gold ornaments looked like lotus blossoms.  The impressions left by their jewelry on their skin resembled additional adornments.  The edges of their garments, stirred by their breath, fluttered like colorful banners.  Their earrings trembled slightly with each exhalation, and the air was filled with the sweet scent of alcoholic beverages.  Some of Ravana's wives, mistaking other women for Ravana in their drunken state, inadvertently kissed one another. Completely infatuated with Ravana, they found pleasure in this confusion.  The women lay in various positions, using their arms or clothing as pillows, their limbs intertwined. Some rested their heads on each other's bosoms, laps, or breasts. Their bodies and ornaments were so entangled that it was difficult to distinguish one from another.  As Ravana slept soundly, the ever-present lamps seemed to gaze upon the women with unwavering attention, a gaze they dared not hold while Ravana was awake.  Hanuman reflected on the diversity of Ravana’s wives – some were the daughters of sages, Brahmins, demons, Gandharvas, and ogres, all captivated by Ravana's allure. Some he had captured in battle, while others, consumed by passion, had willingly joined his harem.  With the exception of Sita, none had been taken against their will; they were won over by Ravana's power, prowess, or charm.  None desired other men, nor had they belonged to others previously. They were all of noble birth, beautiful, graceful, adorned, strong, and pleasing to Ravana.  Hanuman concluded that Sita was superior to them all in every way, and that Ravana's abduction of her was a cruel and dishonorable act.

__data__.text: Hanuman observed a magnificent crystal dais adorned with precious stones, resembling a celestial structure.  Upon the dais was a valuable couch crafted from cat’s-eye gems, ivory, and gold, decorated with painted figures and covered with luxurious bedding.  A white canopy, reminiscent of the moon, hung above, adorned with heavenly wreaths. Nearby, another exquisite couch, overlaid with gold and as radiant as fire, was draped with Asoka flower garlands. Women fanned the area with chowries, and the air was filled with various perfumes and incense.  The couch was covered with a fine bed, upholstered with sheepskin, and decorated with flower wreaths. Hanuman then saw Ravana, asleep on the magnificent couch.  He was adorned with shining earrings and golden robes, his skin like a cloud reddened by the setting sun, his body smeared with fragrant red sandal-paste.  Covered in celestial ornaments, the shapeshifting Ravana, with his many arms, resembled Mount Mandara covered in trees and shrubs.  He had retired after a night of revelry, adorned in jewels, beloved by ogre maids, and a source of joy to ogres.  Having drunk his fill, he lay in deep slumber. Disgusted by the sight of Ravana snoring, Hanuman recoiled.  Moving to a landing on the stairway, he continued to observe the drunken ogre king.  The magnificent couch, with the sleeping Ravana upon it, resembled the majestic Mount Prasravana with a scent-elephant resting on its peak.

Furthermore, she would not consort with another, even a god, as none were equal to Rama.  Hanuman searched the banquet hall again. He observed women in various states of repose, some exhausted from gambling, singing, dancing, or drinking.  Some reclined on musical instruments or beds.  Hanuman saw thousands of beautifully adorned women discussing each other's beauty and the meaning of songs, demonstrating their understanding of etiquette and proper expression, and clearly enjoying themselves. He also observed other sleeping women elsewhere who shared similar qualities.  Among them, Ravana stood out, like a bull among cows or an elephant surrounded by females.  Hanuman continued searching the opulent hall, furnished with every imaginable object.  He noted platters of deer, buffalo, and boar meat, along with untouched peacock and fowl served in large gold vessels.

Hanuman again searched the banquet hall, noting the untouched platters of deer, buffalo, boar, peacock, and fowl. He observed a variety of other partially eaten meats, including boar, rhinoceros, porcupine, deer, peacock, and various birds, goats, hares, buffalo, fish, and ram, all prepared with curds, spices, and sauces.  Drinks of all kinds, including those made from sugar, honey, flowers, and fruits, lay scattered about.  Discarded jewelry, drinking vessels, and flower offerings littered the floor, which shimmered with the light reflecting off gold and crystal containers.  Hanuman saw full, half-full, and empty wine vessels made of gold, silver, and gems.  The scene suggested recent revelry. He observed some women asleep on couches and others lying on the floor, their garlands and coverings slightly moving with their breaths. As Hanuman looked upon the sleeping women, he worried he had committed a sin by seeing other men's wives. He reassured himself that his gaze was free of lust and his observations were necessary for his mission.

He saw leftover food, including various meats and other dishes prepared with curds, spices, and sauces.  The air was still fragrant with the scents of sandalwood, incense, wine, and flowers. Hanuman continued his exploration of the Asoka grove, discovering various ponds filled with clear water. These ponds were unique in shape and size, some featuring gem-encrusted steps and shimmering with pearl and coral sands.  Lotus and lily pads floated on the surface, while the calls of red geese, Cataka birds, swans, and cranes echoed through the air.  Streams flowed into the ponds, their waters as clear as nectar.  Climbing vines and flowering Santana trees draped over the banks, obscuring the view, save for glimpses through the Karavira trees.

A towering mountain, its peak reaching skyward like a rain cloud, caught Hanuman's eye.  Caves dotted its slopes, which were covered in a diverse array of trees. A river cascaded down the mountainside, resembling a woman leaping from her lover's embrace, her descent momentarily halted by the outstretched branches of trees.  Further on, Hanuman saw the river's flow reverse as if the woman had returned to her beloved.  Nearby, lotus ponds teemed with a variety of birds.

Hanuman then came across a large, man-made pond filled with cool water, its steps crafted from precious gems and its bottom lined with pearls. Herds of deer roamed amidst the surrounding thickets and grand mansions designed by Viswakarma. Trees laden with flowers and fruit offered shade from the sun, their bases adorned with golden platforms.  A striking golden Asoka tree, entwined with vines and abundant leaves, stood out, encircled by golden daisies.  Hanuman also noted stretches of open land, mountain springs, and other radiant golden trees that shone like fire.  The brilliance of these trees, reminiscent of Mount Meru, made Hanuman feel as though he himself was bathed in gold.

The trees, laden with seasonal flowers and fruit, created a radiant spectacle, like a sunrise.  Birds flitted among the branches.

The grove boasted a variety of trees: Asoka trees with cascading flowers, Karnikara and Kimsuka trees heavy with blossoms, Punnaga, Saptaparna, Campaka, and Uddalaka trees.  Some Asoka trees shimmered like gold, others like fire, and still others were dark as kohl.  This magnificent grove surpassed even the celestial gardens in beauty and splendor, its flowers like stars in a second sky.

Within this fragrant grove, similar to the mountain Gandhamadana, Hanuman spotted a magnificent white temple, supported by a thousand pillars.  Its coral steps and golden platforms seemed to touch the heavens.  There, surrounded by ogresses, he saw a woman.  Emaciated and sorrowful, she sighed repeatedly.  Her form, though obscured, radiated a subtle beauty.  Clad in a single, worn yellow garment, devoid of adornment, she resembled a lotus pond stripped of its flowers.

Suffering and grief-stricken, she appeared like the star Rohini afflicted by Mars.  Tearful and weakened by fasting, she was consumed by sorrow and anxiety.  Unable to see her loved ones, surrounded only by ogresses, she was like a doe separated from her herd and encircled by hounds.  Her single, dark braid resembled a line of trees against the clear sky after the monsoon rains.

He considered Sita, the daughter of King Janaka, more valuable than the sovereignty of all three worlds. He described her as virtuous and devoted to her husband, Rama.  He recounted Sita's miraculous birth, emerging from the earth as a field was plowed.  He revered her as the esteemed daughter-in-law of the valiant King Dasaratha.  Now, however, she was held captive by ogresses.  Hanuman lamented Sita's suffering, emphasizing her devotion to Rama, her renunciation of worldly pleasures to follow him into exile, and her unwavering resilience.  He described her inner strength, finding contentment in the forest as she had in the royal palace, and her enduring love for Rama despite her ordeal.  He compared Rama's longing for Sita to a thirsty man's search for water.  Hanuman was certain that Rama's joy upon Sita's return would be immense, like a king reclaiming his lost kingdom.  Despite her hardships and isolation, Sita remained steadfast, focused on reuniting with her husband.  Her only focus was Rama, oblivious to her surroundings. Hanuman observed that a husband is a woman's greatest ornament, and Sita, separated from Rama, had lost her radiance.  He also marveled at Rama's strength in enduring the separation from his beloved wife.

The flowers adorning them wilted from the heat of their bodies. Driven by both respect and a desire to see Sita, these women with captivating eyes trailed their lord. He observed the elaborately adorned Ravana, surrounded by torchbearers and engulfed in a cloud of fragrant oil, his arrogance and desire evident.  His gaze, sharp and intense, resembled that of the god of love himself.  As Ravana adjusted his pearl-encrusted garment, which had caught on his armlet, Hanuman, concealed amongst the leaves and flowers of a tree, watched intently, trying to discern who this imposing figure was. He also saw Ravana's beautiful, youthful wives.  Surrounded by this retinue, Ravana entered the lively Asoka grove, filled with the sounds of birds and deer.

She urged him to turn his attention to his own wives and abandon his pursuit of her.  Sita emphasized her devotion to Rama and stated that, like a sinner unable to achieve enlightenment, Ravana was unworthy of her. Born into nobility and married into a pious family, she would never commit such a disgraceful act.  Turning her back to him, Sita reiterated that she was another man's wife and could never be his. She implored Ravana to consider the virtuous path and protect other women as he would his own. She warned that pursuing another’s wife would only lead to humiliation and ruin, citing that kingdoms fall when ruled by those who lack self-control.  Sita predicted Lanka's destruction due to Ravana’s actions and asserted that the world would celebrate the downfall of one so consumed by sin.  Finally, she declared that neither power nor wealth could tempt her, for her bond with Rama was as inseparable as sunlight from the sun.

He boasted, perversely, that this "love" was the reason he hadn't yet killed her, despite her supposed ascetic devotion and insulting words. Emboldened, Sita rebuked Ravana again, questioning the lack of counsel around him to prevent such a vile act and reminding him of Rama's power and her unwavering loyalty.  She declared that no one, other than Ravana, would dare consider such a proposal towards the wife of Rama.  She warned him that such a sinful proposition to the consort of such a powerful being would not go unpunished.

She warned him that such a sinful act against the consort of such a powerful being would bring devastating consequences.  Sita compared Rama to a mighty elephant and Ravana to a mere hare, highlighting the difference in their strength and stature. She mocked Ravana's boldness in insulting Rama while he was absent, suggesting he would never dare speak such words in Rama's presence.  Sita then expressed disbelief that Ravana's eyes had not fallen out from their sockets from the audacity of his lustful gaze upon her.  She also questioned how his tongue had not withered and fallen off for daring to speak so disrespectfully to the wife of such a righteous man and the daughter-in-law of King Dasaratha.  Sita stated that she refrained from reducing him to ashes with her own power only out of respect for Rama's wishes and her own ascetic discipline. Finally, Sita declared her abduction was destiny's way of ensuring Ravana's destruction, questioning why he, with all his supposed power and resources, would resort to such a cowardly act of stealing Rama's wife after tricking him into leaving the hermitage.  Upon hearing this, Ravana, a figure of imposing stature and menacing appearance, turned his angry gaze upon Sita.

__data__.text: Some of Ravana's demonic guards, enraged by Sita's defiance, threatened to report her to Ravana.  They then approached Sita, issuing cruel threats and promising to devour her.  However, the old demoness Trijata, awakened from a dream, intervened, forbidding them from harming Sita, Janaka’s daughter and Rama's beloved wife. Trijata recounted a vivid dream foretelling Rama's triumph and the ogres' destruction. The dream depicted Rama, adorned in white, arriving with Lakshmana in a magnificent ivory palanquin drawn by a thousand horses. Sita, also in white, was seen atop a white mountain surrounded by the sea, reunited with Rama like sunlight with the sun. Rama and Lakshmana, radiant as the sun, then stood beside her, mounted on a massive four-tusked elephant.  Sita, perched on Rama's shoulders, touched the sun and moon.  The elephant, carrying the three of them, then stood upon Lanka.  Another dream showed Rama, again in white, arriving with Sita and Lakshmana in a chariot pulled by eight white bullocks. Yet another dream revealed the valiant Rama, traveling north in the sun-bright aerial car, Pushpaka, with Sita and Lakshmana. Trijata asserted that the mighty Rama was invincible, impossible to defeat by any being. Her dream also showed Ravana, shaven-headed, oil-covered, dressed in red, drunk and adorned with oleander garlands, falling from the Pushpaka car.  He was then seen, disoriented and crazed, riding a donkey southwards, before falling again, terrified and bewildered, leaping up in a frenzy, naked and ranting.

__data__.text: Trijata, interpreting her dream, saw not misfortune upon Sita, but merely a temporary dimming of her radiance, likely due to her captivity and lack of proper care. She envisioned Sita's imminent triumph, along with Ravana's downfall and Rama's victory.  Trijata pointed to physical signs on Sita's body – a throbbing left eye, a trembling left arm, and a twitching left thigh – as further positive omens, foretelling good news and Rama's return.  A bird's sweet song further reinforced the positive signs, signifying the arrival of an auspicious time.  Overjoyed by these predictions of her husband's victory and her own liberation, Sita offered her protection to the ogresses if the dream proved true.

__data__.text: Sita, terrified by Ravana's threats and separated from Rama, felt like a trapped elephant calf.  Surrounded by the ogresses and constantly threatened, she lamented her fate, feeling like a child abandoned in a desolate forest.  She questioned why she continued to live, despite the relentless torment.  Though heartbroken, she was surprised her heart hadn't shattered from the pain.  Sita felt that death would be preferable to remaining captive to the ogre, as she could no more give him her affection than a Brahmin could teach sacred verses to someone outside their caste. She believed Ravana would kill her before Rama could arrive, like a surgeon dissecting a lifeless fetus.  The two months she had been given to live seemed to stretch endlessly before her, like the final night of a condemned prisoner.  She cried out to Rama, Lakshmana, Sumitra, Kausalya, and her own mothers, feeling she was about to be destroyed like a boat in a storm.  Sita lamented that Rama and Lakshmana might have been killed because of her, like lions struck by lightning, blaming the golden deer that had lured them away.  She blamed herself for sending them after it, believing it was the Time-Spirit in disguise who had tricked her. She called out to Rama, lamenting that he, a righteous and beloved king, was unaware of her impending doom. Sita felt that her devotion to Rama, her forbearance, her piety, and her fidelity were all in vain, like service rendered to ungrateful people.  Her virtuous life and devotion to her husband seemed meaningless because she was separated from him, pale, emaciated, and hopeless. She imagined Rama returning from exile, successful and free from fear, marrying other women while she, filled with longing for him, would meet her demise, her austerities and vows having been for nothing. She cursed her ill fortune and declared her intention to end her life.

She envisioned Rama returning from exile, marrying other women while she, longing for him, would die, her sacrifices having been in vain.  Desperate, Sita contemplated suicide, wishing for poison or a weapon.  Finding neither in Ravana's fortress, she resolved to hang herself using the cord that bound her hair. As she grasped a branch of the Asoka tree, preparing to end her life, several auspicious omens, known to dispel grief and foretell success, manifested themselves on her person.

Her grief and weariness vanished, replaced by joy and renewed hope.

__data__.text: Hanuman, having heard Sita's lament, Trijata's dream, and the threats of the demonesses, contemplated his next move.  Observing Sita, he realized she was the same one the monkey army sought. He reviewed the information he had gathered: the demons' power, the layout of Lanka, and Ravana's might. He felt compelled to comfort Sita, who longed for her husband, Rama.  He reasoned that if he left without consoling her, his mission would be a failure and Sita might despair and die.  He also worried how he could face Rama without a message from Sita.  He feared Rama's anger if he returned empty-handed and believed that even if Sugriva launched an attack, it would be pointless if Sita were no longer alive. He was determined to speak to her, but recognized the risk of doing so in front of the demonesses, creating a difficult dilemma.  He knew he had to act before the night ended, lest Sita lose all hope.

He also worried about facing Rama without news of Sita, envisioning his lord's anger and the futility of Sugriva's army if Sita were gone.  He resolved to speak to her, despite the risks of discovery by the demonesses.  Hanuman considered his small stature and monkey form, knowing he would have to speak Sanskrit to be understood.  However, he feared speaking the refined language would frighten Sita, who might mistake him for Ravana.  He concluded he must speak the common tongue of Ayodhya to gain her trust.  Even then, he worried his appearance coupled with human speech would further terrify her, leading her to cry out.  This, he feared, would alert the demonesses, who would attack him.  He imagined them surrounding him, their monstrous forms a terrifying sight, and himself fleeing through the trees, his large frame further alarming them. He envisioned the demonesses summoning Ravana’s guards, armed with an array of weapons, adding to the chaos.

__data__.text: Hanuman grappled with the potential consequences of revealing himself to Sita. He imagined leaping through the Ashoka grove, alarming the demonesses with his size and agility.  The commotion would attract Ravana's guards, armed and ready to attack. Surrounded, Hanuman knew he could defeat them, but the battle would exhaust him, preventing his return journey across the ocean. Capture was another possibility, leaving Sita unaware of Rama's search and himself imprisoned.  Even worse, he feared the demonesses, enraged by his presence, might harm Sita.  Such an outcome would devastate Rama and render Sugriva's alliance pointless. Hanuman despaired, seeing Sita isolated and vulnerable in Lanka, with no one else capable of reaching her. He recognized his unique position and the immense responsibility it carried.  He questioned the wisdom of directly speaking to Sita, weighing the risk of discovery against the certainty of her despair if he remained silent.  Hanuman emphasized the importance of careful consideration, recognizing that even well-laid plans could fail through poor execution. He worried his own anxieties might cloud his judgment and sought a course of action that would guarantee success.

__data__.text: Hanuman wrestled with the dilemma of approaching Sita. He feared that speaking to her directly could lead to a grave error, perhaps discovery and ensuing conflict.  Yet, remaining silent carried the heavy risk of deepening her despair, possibly even driving her to take her own life.  He recognized the delicate balance required, acknowledging that even the best plans could fail if poorly executed, particularly if the messenger was timid or lacked good judgment.  He worried about the possibility of failure, questioning how he could best achieve his goal without jeopardizing Sita's safety and ensure his efforts weren't wasted.  After careful consideration, Hanuman resolved to approach Sita cautiously, focusing on reassuring words about Rama.  He planned to speak gently and respectfully, reminding Sita of her noble husband's unwavering love and tireless efforts to find her.  Hanuman decided to deliver Rama's message with carefully chosen words, emphasizing truth and righteousness, hoping to earn Sita's trust and alleviate her suffering.  He settled among the tree branches, preparing to address her.

__data__.text: Hanuman, after much deliberation, spoke kindly to Sita, recounting the story of Rama. He described King Dasaratha, Rama's father, as a virtuous and renowned king, skilled in warfare and comparable to Indra in might.  He further extolled Dasaratha's virtues, highlighting his compassion and ability to bring happiness to his kingdom. Hanuman then introduced Rama, Dasaratha's eldest son, a skilled archer and protector of his people and righteousness. He explained how Rama, along with Sita and his brother Lakshmana, went into exile to honor his father's promise.  In the forest, Rama defeated many shape-shifting ogres.  Upon hearing of this, Ravana, enraged, abducted Sita using trickery.  Rama, searching for Sita, allied with Sugriva, the monkey king. Sugriva's monkey army, including Hanuman, searched for Sita. Hanuman, following a tip from Sampati, leaped across the vast ocean and found Sita, recognizing her by the description Rama had given.  Sita, astonished by Hanuman's words, looked up into the tree where he sat.  Looking around in all directions after hearing Hanuman speak, Sita was filled with joy, constantly thinking of Rama. She then saw Hanuman, son of the wind-god and Sugriva's minister, sitting in the tree, radiant like the rising sun.

__data__.text: Sita, hidden amongst the branches of the Aśoka tree, was startled by the sight of Hanuman, whose white and tawny fur resembled flashes of lightning.  She observed him, noting his gentle demeanor and the way he shone like the blossoms of the Aśoka, his eyes gleaming like refined gold.  A wave of wonder washed over her as she saw the esteemed Hanuman sitting humbly before her.  Initially, Sita was frightened by his imposing figure, fearing him and even momentarily losing consciousness.  She cried out in distress, calling for Rama and Lakshmana.  Upon regaining her senses, Sita wondered if the encounter was merely a dream.  She observed Hanuman carefully, noting his powerful, partially broken jaw, a testament to his youthful encounter with Indra.  The sight of him overwhelmed her again, causing her to faint.  When she awoke, she questioned the reality of the experience, citing the inauspicious nature of seeing a monkey in a dream.  However, she quickly dismissed the idea, reasoning that sleep evaded her grief-stricken mind.  She constantly thought of Rama, spoke his name, and clung to any mention of him. The vividness of the encounter and Hanuman's words made her doubt it was a dream.  She pondered the possibility of a mere apparition, but the monkey's distinct form and speech challenged that notion.  Ultimately, Sita offered a prayer to Brhaspati, Indra, Brahma, and Agni, hoping that Hanuman's words would prove true.

__data__.text: Rama, heartbroken from separation, along with the valiant Lakshmana and their ally, Sugriva, king of the monkeys, have inquired about Sita's well-being. Hanuman, revealing himself as Sugriva's minister, assures Sita, who is thankfully still alive despite her captivity, of her imminent rescue. He boasts of his daring journey across the ocean and into Ravana's city, symbolically claiming dominance over Ravana. Hanuman urges Sita to discard her suspicion and trust his words, emphasizing that he is not what she perceives him to be.

Hanuman assures Sita of his connection to Rama and begins recounting details of Rama and Lakshmana's appearance and character. Sita, still uncertain, asks Hanuman how he came to know them, prompting him to narrate his life story, including his role as Sugriva's minister and his journey to Lanka. He then describes Rama as noble and virtuous: possessing lotus-petal eyes, a moonlike face, and innate charm and generosity. Rama is compared to the sun in brilliance, the earth in patience, the sage Brihaspati in wisdom, and Indra in fame. He is a protector of all beings, upholder of dharma, and champion of his people. He is also depicted as a guardian of social order, defining moral boundaries. Furthermore, Rama is described as radiant, revered, chaste, and supportive of holy men. Skilled in statecraft, a devotee of Brahmins, wise, compassionate, and self-controlled, he is also a formidable warrior.  Hanuman details Rama's mastery of the Vedas, particularly the Yajurveda, and his expertise in archery. Finally, he describes Rama's physical attributes: broad shoulders, powerful arms, a conch-like neck, a pleasant face, coppery eyes, and a well-built physique.

Hanuman continues his detailed description of Rama to reassure Sita. He portrays Rama as a virtuous and radiant figure, steadfast in his chastity and dedicated to righteous actions. Rama is skilled in politics, a devout worshipper of Brahmins, wise, compassionate, and a formidable warrior.  Hanuman emphasizes Rama's mastery of the Vedas and archery. He then provides a thorough account of Rama's physical attributes, from his broad shoulders and powerful arms to his coppery eyes and well-proportioned physique. Hanuman goes on to describe Rama's voice, complexion, and intricate bodily features.  Hanuman also highlights Lakshmana's similar qualities, describing him as a reflection of Rama in affection, charm, and virtues. He recounts how Rama and Lakshmana, grieving Sita's absence, searched for her, eventually allying with Sugriva after witnessing his plight.  Hanuman describes the alliance between Rama and Sugriva to defeat Vali and find Sita.  He concludes this portion of his narrative by stating that Vali was defeated by Rama and Lakshmana upon their arrival in Kiskindha.

Hanuman continues his narrative, describing Rama and Lakshmana's search for Sita.  Radiant and eager to find her, they joined forces with Hanuman and other monkeys.  They encountered Sugriva, the rightful monkey king, who had been overthrown by his brother Vali and was hiding in fear. Hanuman describes Sugriva's appearance and his desperate situation. The brothers, Rama and Lakshmana, then arrived at Mount Rysymuka, armed with their bows.  Seeing them, Sugriva, terrified, fled to the mountain peak and sent Hanuman to assess the situation.  Hanuman approached the brothers respectfully and explained Sugriva's predicament. Relieved and happy to learn the truth, Rama and Lakshmana were then escorted by Hanuman to meet Sugriva.  Later, Hanuman describes how he revived a despairing Sugriva. He then reiterates that he stands before Sita as an envoy for the allied Rama and Sugriva. Following the alliance, Sugriva rallied his monkey army and dispatched them in all directions to search for Sita. Hanuman and his group, fearful of disobeying Sugriva, diligently searched but became lost on the Vindhyan mountains.  Dejected and fearing Sugriva's wrath after the passage of time, they nearly gave up hope.

Hanuman recounts how he revived the grieving Sugriva.  Rama and Lakshmana examined Sita's jewels, which they entrusted to Sugriva for safekeeping. Hanuman emphasizes Rama's profound sorrow over Sita's absence, comparing it to a raging fire and a devastating earthquake.  Rama finds no joy in the beautiful forests and rivers without Sita.  Hanuman then details previous events: Rama and Sugriva formed an alliance after sharing their stories. Lakshmana informed Sugriva of Rama's grief, causing Sugriva to appear despondent.  The monkeys presented Rama with Sita’s jewels, found scattered on the ground.  Overcome with emotion, Rama wept. Hanuman then describes the encounter with Sampati, Jatayu's brother, who revealed Sita's location in Ravana's abode.  Energized by this news, the monkeys, led by Angada, journeyed to the seashore. Hanuman reminds Sita that he has seen both her and Ravana, and that he has recounted these events truthfully. He urges her to speak, identifying himself as Rama's messenger, Sugriva's minister, and the son of the wind-god, assuring her of Rama's well-being.

Hanuman consoles Sita, assuring her that Rama deeply mourns her absence, finding no solace in nature's beauty. He vows that Rama will defeat Ravana and rescue her.  He recounts the alliance between Rama and Sugriva, forged to defeat Vali and search for Sita.  After Vali's death, Sugriva became king and dispatched search parties in all directions. Hanuman explains he is part of this mission, sent by Sugriva, and his discovery of Sita will bring relief to the searching monkeys.  He adds that finding Sita will bring him renown and anticipates Rama's victory over Ravana. He introduces himself as Hanuman, son of Kesari and the wind-god, born on a sacred mountain.  Sita, convinced by Hanuman's words and evident proofs, feels immense relief and joy, her face radiant like the moon emerging from an eclipse.

Angada and the monkey search party, failing to find Sita, resolved to fast to death.  Overcome with grief, Angada lamented Sita's disappearance, Vali's death, and their own impending demise.  Sampati, Jatayu's brother, providentially appeared.  He learned of Jatayu's death while fighting Ravana for Sita and revealed Sita's location in Ravana's abode in Lanka.  Inspired by this news, the monkeys journeyed to the seashore.  Hanuman, dispelling the monkeys' fear of the vast ocean, leaped across to Lanka.  He reassured Sita, offering further assistance and requesting permission to leave.  He then reiterated his lineage, born of the wind-god after Kesari defeated Sambasadana.

Hanuman reassures Sita, detailing his journey and the monkey army's despair at the vast ocean. He recounts entering Lanka, seeing Ravana, and finding Sita in her sorrowful state.  He identifies himself as Rama's messenger, sent by Sugriva, and affirms Rama and Lakshmana's well-being and devotion to her. Hanuman explains his solo mission, driven by Sugriva's command and his shapeshifting ability, and rejoices in his success, promising to inform the anxious monkeys of her discovery. He assures Sita of the renown he will gain and of Rama's imminent arrival to defeat Ravana and his forces, rescuing her. He relates his lineage, born of the wind-god and Kesari's consort, after Kesari's heroic defeat of Sambasadana.  He emphasizes his fame as Hanuman and reiterates Rama's virtues to bolster her confidence in her imminent rescue.

Hanuman consoles Sita, recounting Rama's virtues and promising her imminent rescue by her husband.  Sita, convinced by Hanuman's words and proofs, feels immense relief and joy, her face radiant.  Acknowledging Hanuman as a monkey messenger, Sita listens as he offers to fulfill any further requests before departing.  Hanuman then briefly reiterates his lineage, highlighting his birth after Kesari's victory over Sambasadana.

Finally, she questions whether Bharata will send an army and if Sugriva and his monkey forces, along with Lakshmana, will come to her aid.  She expresses her hope of witnessing Ravana's defeat at Rama's hands.

Hanuman assures Sita that she will be reunited with Rama soon.

He assures Sita that Rama would overcome any obstacle, even death itself, to reach her.  He paints a vivid picture of Rama's sorrow, comparing his unrest to a wounded elephant. He swears by various mountains and their resources that Sita will soon see Rama again, emphasizing his handsome features. Hanuman describes Rama's austere lifestyle, abstaining from meat and honey, consuming only simple fruits and rice.  He portrays Rama's distraction and inability to focus on even mundane tasks, his mind consumed by thoughts of Sita. He reveals that Rama constantly calls out Sita's name, even in his sleep, and sighs longingly at the sight of anything that reminds him of her.  Hanuman emphasizes Rama's unwavering devotion and his tireless efforts to find and retrieve her. Upon hearing these words, Sita's initial despair is replaced by a mix of relief and sorrow – relief at Rama's love and efforts, yet sorrow for his suffering. This emotional duality is compared to a partly cloudy night during autumn.

She worried about the time limit imposed by Ravana and expressed her doubt that Rama could defeat Ravana and rescue her before it expired. She recounted how Ravana had ignored Vibhisana's pleas to return her to Rama.  Sita shared information about Kala, Vibhisana's daughter, and Avindhya, a wise and respected Rakshasa, who had also tried to persuade Ravana but failed. __data__.text: Sita recounted to Hanuman a specific incident to relay to Rama as proof of their encounter.  While residing in a hermitage near Citrakita mountain, Sita, after bathing, sat upon Rama's lap.  A crow, drawn by the scent of flesh, began pecking at her.  Sita attempted to ward off the crow with a clod of earth, but the persistent bird continued its attack.  As Sita adjusted her clothing, her skirt slipped, momentarily exposing her, a moment Rama witnessed with amusement, causing Sita embarrassment.  The crow, still hungry, pecked at her again, and she sought comfort in Rama's lap.  Exhausted, Sita fell asleep in Rama's embrace.  While they slept, the crow returned and clawed at Sita's breasts.  Awakening to Sita's cries, Rama, seeing her wounds and enraged, questioned who dared harm her. He then spotted the crow, perched nearby, its claws bloody.  Sita explained that this crow, renowned for its speed, was said to be the son of Indra.

__data__.text: Sita continued her narration to Hanuman, describing Rama's reaction to the crow's attack.  Seeing Sita's wounds, Rama was enraged, demanding to know who had harmed her.  He quickly spotted the crow perched nearby, its claws bloody. Sita explained this was Indra's son, known for his incredible speed. Furious, Rama plucked a blade of kusa grass and imbued it with the power of Brahma's weapon.  The grass blazed like a catastrophic fire and was flung at the crow. The fiery blade pursued the crow relentlessly as it fled across the three worlds, seeking refuge with Indra and the great sages, but finding none.  Finally, it returned to Rama, falling at his feet and begging for mercy. Though the crow deserved death, Rama, ever compassionate, offered it a chance to live. He declared that Brahma's weapon could not be recalled, but its effect could be mitigated.  The crow then sacrificed its right eye to the fiery blade, and its life was spared.  Having bowed to Rama and his father, Dasaratha, the crow was released and returned home. Sita, addressing an imagined Rama, lamented, "You unleashed Brahma's weapon on a mere crow for my sake. How then can you tolerate the one who abducted me from you?" She pleaded with him to show her compassion, for though she had a protector in him, she felt utterly abandoned.

She also requested Hanuman to inquire about Lakshmana's welfare, describing him as a noble, selfless warrior who forsook worldly pleasures and comforts to support Rama in exile.  Sita highlighted Lakshmana's strength, devotion to his brother, and respect for her, recalling his ignorance of her abduction. She emphasized Lakshmana's importance in her rescue, urging Hanuman to deliver her message carefully so that Lakshmana, the ever-mild and clever one, would understand her plight and act to end her suffering. Sita declared her resolve to survive only for a month more, urging Rama to rescue her from Ravana's clutches. She then gave Hanuman her head jewel as a token for Rama, which Hanuman respectfully accepted. Filled with joy at finding Sita, Hanuman prepared to return, carrying Sita's message and token.

She points out that such a feat is typically only achievable by divine beings like Garuda, the wind-god, or Hanuman himself.  Sita questions Hanuman, whom she recognizes for his wisdom and resourcefulness, about his plan to overcome this significant obstacle.  While acknowledging Hanuman’s individual capability to rescue her, Sita emphasizes that a victory achieved solely by him wouldn't bring the same glory to Rama as a victory achieved with his entire army. She envisions a triumphant Rama returning to his capital after conquering Ravana with the combined might of his forces, and expresses her desire for this outcome.  Sita urges Hanuman to devise a plan that allows Rama to showcase his valor and strength appropriately.  Upon hearing Sita’s concerns, Hanuman responds by assuring her of Sugriva’s commitment to her rescue.  He describes the monkey army as a powerful force, readily awaiting Sugriva’s command, capable of traversing vast distances and undeterred by any obstacle.  Hanuman reveals that the army has already circumnavigated the earth multiple times and includes individuals as powerful, and even more powerful, than himself. He implies that his own presence there signifies the imminent arrival of the rest of the army, as superior warriors like himself are not typically sent on preliminary missions.

__data__.text: Hanuman continues to reassure Sita, describing the monkey army's immense power and unwavering loyalty to Sugriva.  He emphasizes their extraordinary physical abilities, highlighting their capacity for effortless leaps and bounds, their tireless energy, and their unwavering determination.  Hanuman recounts their past feats, mentioning how they have circumnavigated the earth multiple times.  He subtly boasts about his own prowess, stating that while there are monkeys as strong or even stronger than him in the army, none are his inferior.  He uses his own presence as proof of the army's imminent arrival, arguing that superior warriors like himself are not typically sent as mere messengers.  Hanuman then comforts Sita directly, urging her to cast aside her grief and assuring her of the monkey leaders' swift arrival in Lanka.  He promises to personally carry Rama and Lakshmana on his back, likening their arrival to the rising sun and moon.  He foretells Rama’s victory over Ravana and his triumphant return to Ayodhya with Sita.  Hanuman encourages Sita to remain hopeful, promising her that she will soon be reunited with Rama.  He paints a vivid picture of the monkey army's impending assault on Lanka, describing them as fierce warriors resembling lions and tigers, and as imposing as elephants, utilizing their natural weapons – nails and teeth.  He portrays them thundering across the mountains of Lanka, their numbers vast and their presence awe-inspiring.  Finally, Hanuman reminds Sita of Rama's own eagerness to rescue her, comparing his restless state to a lion-wounded elephant.

He describes the monkey army, comparing their strength and ferocity to lions and tigers, their imposing size to elephants, and their natural weaponry to sharp nails and teeth.  He depicts them as a vast force, thundering across Lanka's mountains, resembling moving mountains and clouds.  He emphasizes Rama's own distress and impatience to be reunited with her, comparing him to an elephant wounded by a lion.  Hanuman urges Sita to cease her grieving and fear, assuring her of a swift reunion with Rama, just as the goddess Sachi was reunited with Indra. He extols the unmatched virtues of Rama and Lakshmana, highlighting them as her protectors. Finally, he reassures her that her stay in Lanka will be short-lived, asking her to remain patient only until he can inform Rama of her plight.

__data__.text: After leaving Sita, Hanuman contemplated his next move.  He decided that a display of strength was necessary to assess the Rakshasas’ power.  He reasoned that diplomacy, gifts, or sowing discord wouldn't work against the arrogant, wealthy Rakshasas.  He believed that defeating their key warriors would force them to reveal their true strength. Hanuman felt he would only fulfill his mission if he returned to Sugriva having assessed the enemy's power and formulated a plan. He wondered how he could provoke a confrontation and force Ravana to reveal his army's might. Hanuman planned to observe Ravana, his advisors, army, and charioteer to understand their strategies.  He decided to destroy Ravana’s beautiful pleasure garden, provoking a reaction.  Hanuman anticipated that Ravana would retaliate with his formidable army, creating an opportunity for Hanuman to evaluate their strength in battle.  He then planned to return to Sugriva after defeating the ogre army.  With this plan, the powerful Hanuman began to demolish the garden's trees. He destroyed the pleasure garden, which was filled with various trees, plants, and the sounds of agitated birds.

__data__.text: Hanuman, anticipating a fierce battle, reasoned that Ravana would deploy his vast army, equipped with various weapons, against him.  He was confident that he could single-handedly defeat Ravana's forces and return to Sugriva.  Filled with immense strength and speed, Hanuman began to tear down the trees in Ravana's pleasure garden.  He completely devastated the garden, leaving it a chaotic mess of uprooted trees, muddy ponds, and damaged hills. The once beautiful garden, filled with diverse trees, creepers, and the sounds of birds, was now a desolate and unsightly scene, resembling an area ravaged by wildfire.  The destruction extended to the garden's structures, including arbors, galleries, and grottos, leaving them in ruins and causing distress to the animals within.  The garden, once a place of beauty and tranquility, became a source of sorrow, its once vibrant Ashoka creepers now symbols of despair.  Having achieved his goal of provoking Ravana, Hanuman, radiating with power and ready for battle, positioned himself at the garden's entrance.

These fearsome ogres, eager for battle, charged towards Hanuman, who awaited them at the archway, like moths drawn to a flame.

__data__.text: Ravana dispatched eighty thousand Kinkara warriors, armed with iron mallets and clubs, to subdue Hanuman.  These ogres, described as having large bellies, teeth, and terrifying forms, eagerly advanced towards Hanuman, who stood his ground at the archway. The Kinkaras attacked Hanuman with maces, gold-plated clubs, and arrows.  They surrounded him, wielding sharp spears, iron pikes, lances, and javelins.  In response, Hanuman roared loudly and, expanding to a gigantic size, slammed his tail against the ground, creating a sound that reverberated through Lanka and startled the birds from the sky. He proclaimed his allegiance to Rama and Sugriva, declaring himself a servant of Rama and capable of defeating countless Ravanas. He vowed to destroy Lanka, see Sita, and return safely, despite the ogres' presence.  His roar terrified the Kinkaras, who now recognized him as Rama's messenger and attacked him with even greater ferocity.  Hanuman, surrounded, grabbed a large iron bar from the archway.

He realized that while he had ravaged the royal garden, the sanctuary dedicated to the ogres' guardian deity remained untouched. Declaring his intent to demolish it, he effortlessly scaled the towering structure, which resembled the mighty Mount Meru.  Atop the sanctuary, the radiant Hanuman shone like a second sun.  His presence blazed with an indomitable aura as he began to dismantle the edifice, the crashing sounds echoing throughout Lanka, causing birds and guards to fall senseless.  While demolishing the structure, Hanuman proclaimed the victory of Rama and Lakshmana, and the triumph of Sugriva under Rama's protection. He declared himself a servant of Rama and boasted of his unmatched strength, asserting that not even a thousand Ravanas could withstand his power. He vowed to destroy Lanka, greet Sita, and return triumphant, while the ogres watched helplessly.  With this declaration, Hanuman roared thunderously, terrifying the ogre population.

__data__.text: Canto XLIV begins with Ravana dispatching his warrior, Jambumali, son of Prahasta, to capture Hanuman. Jambumali, adorned in red attire and jewelry, wields a powerful bow, its twang echoing like thunder.  Hanuman, observing Jambumali's arrival in a donkey-drawn chariot, roars in anticipation of the battle.  Jambumali attacks Hanuman with arrows, striking him in the face, head, and arms.  Despite the assault, Hanuman's face, stained with blood, is described as beautiful.  Angered, Hanuman hurls a large rock at Jambumali, who shatters it with arrows.  Hanuman then uproots a sal tree and whirls it as a weapon, but Jambumali destroys the tree with more arrows, also wounding Hanuman's chest and arms.  Enraged and covered in arrows, Hanuman grabs his iron club, preparing to retaliate.

__data__.text: Hanuman, witnessing his efforts thwarted, uprooted a massive sal tree and began to whirl it menacingly. Jambumali responded by showering Hanuman with arrows, cleaving the tree and wounding the monkey's arms, chest, and torso.  Enraged and bristling with arrows, Hanuman grabbed his iron club and, with furious strength, swung it at Jambumali's chest with tremendous force. The blow was so devastating that Jambumali, his chariot, and even his donkeys were utterly obliterated, leaving no trace.  News of Jambumali's death and the slaughter of his soldiers reached Ravana, who flew into a rage.  His eyes burning with fury, he immediately ordered the sons of his chief minister, renowned for their strength and prowess, to confront Hanuman.

__data__.text:
Hanuman, after defeating the Kinkaras, climbed back atop the archway.  Ravana, enraged, dispatched seven of his chief minister's sons along with a massive army to confront him.  These warriors, adorned in gold and wielding powerful bows, rode chariots decorated with banners and flags, creating a thunderous noise.  Their mothers and families, learning of the Kinkaras' fate, were overcome with grief and fear.

The minister's sons, eager to prove themselves, charged towards Hanuman, showering him with arrows.  Hanuman, momentarily obscured by the volley of projectiles, skillfully evaded the attack, moving swiftly through the sky. He toyed with his adversaries, much like the wind-god plays amongst the clouds.  With a mighty roar that terrified the enemy ranks, Hanuman launched his counterattack.  He struck some with his palms and feet, others with his fists, and tore some apart with his nails.  Some were crushed against his chest and thighs, while others simply collapsed from the force of his roar.  The minister's sons defeated, the remaining army scattered in terror.  Elephants trumpeted, horses fell, and the battlefield became littered with broken chariots.

__data__.text: Hanuman continued his assault, striking down Ravana's warriors with his hands, feet, fists, and nails. Some were crushed against his powerful chest and thighs, while others simply collapsed from the force of his roar.  With the minister's sons defeated, the remaining army panicked and fled in all directions.  Elephants trumpeted, horses fell, and the battlefield was littered with broken chariots.  Blood flowed, staining the ground.  The cries of the fleeing demons filled Lanka.  Victorious, Hanuman returned to the archway, ready to face any further challengers.

__data__.text: Ravana, upon learning of Hanuman's devastating attack and the death of his chief minister's sons, devises a new strategy. Recognizing Hanuman's extraordinary power, Ravana suspects that he is more than just a monkey.  He dispatches five powerful generals – Virupaksha, Yupaksa, Durdhara, Praghasa, and Bhasakarna – with a vast army of horses, chariots, and elephants to capture Hanuman.  Ravana cautions his generals to be wary of Hanuman's strength, speed, and intellect, comparing him to a powerful being disguised as a monkey. He even speculates that Hanuman might be a celestial entity sent by Indra to destroy them, reminding his generals of their past victories against gods, demons, and sages.  Ravana emphasizes the importance of capturing Hanuman and not underestimating his abilities. He recalls witnessing other powerful monkeys like Vali, Sugriva, Jambavan, and Nila, but none possessed the same level of power and skill as Hanuman. He concludes that Hanuman must be a formidable being in disguise.

__data__.text: Ravana, recalling his encounters with powerful monkeys like Vali, Sugriva, Jambavan, and Nila, notes that none possessed Hanuman's exceptional strength, speed, and intellect. He concludes Hanuman must be a formidable being disguised as a monkey.  Ravana commands his five generals – Virupaksha, Yupaksa, Durdhara, Praghasa, and Bhasakarna – to capture Hanuman, emphasizing the importance of this mission and the uncertainty of battle. The generals, armed and energized, advance with their forces. They encounter Hanuman, radiating a brilliant aura, and attack him from all sides.  Durdhara strikes Hanuman with five arrows, but they affect him no more than flower petals. Hanuman leaps into the sky, his roar echoing in all directions.  Durdhara attacks with a volley of arrows, but Hanuman deflects them with his roar.  Enraged, Hanuman grows in size and leaps onto Durdhara's chariot with the force of a thunderbolt.

__data__.text: Hanuman, facing Durdhara's relentless arrow attack, countered the assault with a powerful roar that deflected the projectiles.  Growing in size and strength, Hanuman then leaped onto Durdhara's chariot with devastating force, destroying it and killing the general.  Enraged by this, Virupaksha and Yupaksa attacked Hanuman in the air, striking him with clubs.  Hanuman countered their attack and descended to the ground, uprooting a sal tree and slaying both generals with it.  Next, Praghasa attacked with a spear and Bhasakarna with a dart, wounding Hanuman.  Burning with rage, Hanuman tore off a mountain peak, complete with its flora and fauna, and crushed the two remaining generals. With all five generals defeated, Hanuman turned his attention to the remaining enemy forces, single-handedly decimating them with their own weapons and vehicles.

__data__.text: Hanuman, wounded but enraged by the attacks of Virupaksha and Yupaksa, retaliated with immense force. He uprooted a mountain peak, complete with its wildlife and vegetation, and used it to crush the two generals. With the five generals appointed by Ravana now dead, Hanuman turned his attention to the remaining enemy troops. He single-handedly devastated the remaining forces, using their own weapons and chariots against them. The battlefield became choked with the bodies of the fallen soldiers, horses, elephants, and wrecked chariots.  Victorious, Hanuman returned to his position at the archway, awaiting his next opportunity to demonstrate his strength and prowess, like a force of nature poised to unleash further destruction.

__data__.text: Ravana's son, Aksa, a skilled warrior adorned with gold, eagerly entered the battlefield. Riding a magnificent chariot, radiant as the sun, he confronted Hanuman. Hanuman, initially surprised by Aksa's youth, observed the prince's confidence.  Aksa, fueled by pride and ambition, attacked Hanuman with three arrows.  Hanuman, though struck and bleeding, remained formidable, his resilience evident.  The clash of these two powerful warriors shook the very foundations of the world – the earth trembled, the sun dimmed, the wind stilled, the mountains quaked, the sky resounded, and the sea churned.  Aksa, skilled in archery, continued his assault, striking Hanuman with three more arrows, but Hanuman’s strength and determination remained unbroken.

__data__.text: Aksa, adorned in gold, faced Hanuman in a momentous clash that awed even gods and demons.  The earth trembled, the sun dimmed, and the wind stilled as they fought. Aksa, a skilled archer, struck Hanuman with three arrows, but Hanuman remained unyielding. Aksa, displaying remarkable archery skills, continued his assault, striking Hanuman’s head with three more arrows, but Hanuman's resilience shone through, appearing like the rising sun despite his wounds.  Witnessing Aksa’s skill and determination, Hanuman, invigorated, grew in size and retaliated with fiery energy. Aksa, likened to a storm cloud, rained arrows upon Hanuman.  Impressed by the young prince's prowess, Hanuman roared with delight.  Aksa, driven by youthful enthusiasm and rage, continued his relentless attack. Hanuman, struck by Aksa's arrows, roared mightily and stretched his limbs, preparing for a counter-offensive. Aksa pursued Hanuman into the air, showering him with arrows. Hanuman, with his remarkable speed, deftly evaded the arrows. Observing Aksa’s skill and courage, Hanuman paused, filled with respect for the young warrior. Wounded by Aksa's arrows, Hanuman contemplated the prince's extraordinary abilities and considered the appropriate course of action.  He recognized Aksa’s exceptional talent and strength, and felt reluctant to harm such a remarkable young warrior. Hanuman reflected on Aksa’s noble character, his unwavering focus, and the respect he commanded even from wise hermits and supernatural beings.

__data__.text: Hanuman, observing Aksa’s impressive display of archery, paused thoughtfully.  Struck by Aksa’s arrows, Hanuman roared and considered his next move. He admired the young prince's strength and skill, reluctant to harm such a promising warrior.  Aksa, confident and unwavering, met Hanuman’s gaze.  Hanuman realized that if he hesitated, Aksa might gain the upper hand. Deciding to act, Hanuman swiftly killed Aksa’s eight chariot horses.  Aksa's chariot crashed to the ground, and the prince leaped into the air, armed with his bow and sword.  Hanuman, matching Aksa’s speed, caught him by the legs and, after spinning him around, threw him to the ground.  Aksa was killed, his body broken. Hanuman’s victory was witnessed by gods, demons, and wise hermits, all astonished by his power.  Hanuman then returned to the archway, awaiting his next opportunity to strike against Ravana’s forces.

__data__.text: Indrajit, a skilled warrior, used Brahma's powerful missile to capture Hanuman. Believing Hanuman was invulnerable, Indrajit bound him, causing him to fall unconscious.  Hanuman, realizing the missile's divine origin and recalling a boon from Brahma, understood he would be freed shortly. He chose to remain bound, recognizing it as a way to meet Ravana.  The ogres, seeing Hanuman immobile, bound him with ropes. Hanuman accepted this, believing it would further pique Ravana's curiosity and ensure a meeting. However, Brahma's missile's power automatically released Hanuman from its effect upon being bound by the ropes, a fact unknown to the ogres or Indrajit.  Indrajit, seeing Hanuman acting as if still under the missile's influence despite being tied with ropes, realized the ogres' actions had inadvertently broken the missile's hold, frustrating his plan.

Canto IX

Kaikeyi, whose heart was poisoned by the malicious gossip of Manthara as
aforesaid, takes a vow to see that Rama is sent into exile and Bharata
installed as Prince Regent, and asks Manthara herself how to
secure that consummation. Manthara tells her how in the
course of a conflict between gods and demons, in which
Dasaratha’s help was enlisted by the gods, the queen,
who had accompanied her husband to the field of
operations and had rendered valuable assistance
to him at a critical juncture, was offered a couple
of boons, which she had kept in abeyance.

Manthara now asks Kaikeyi to demand the
banishment of Rama and the installation of
Bharata against the two promised boons.

Kaikeyi accordingly throws away her
ornaments and lies down on the bare
floor in the sulking-room in
a sullen mood

usher in Sri Rama with his consort. Seeing the Emperor fall unconscious
at the very sight of the heir-apparent, the ladies of the royal household
start wailing piteously. On Sri Rama’s soliciting his permission to
retire to the woods, the king enjoins him to take his father
captive and ascend the throne. Sri Rama in his turn
consoles his father by assuring him that he has no
hankering for royal fortune and that to him
obedience to his father’s command is of
utmost importance. Dasaratha, however,
falls unconscious again at the very thought
of his separation from Sri Rama and
Sumantra as well as all the ladies of
the gynaeceum follow suit

Apprised of Sri Rama’s arrival by Sumantra, Dagaratha commands him to
usher in Sri Rama with his consort. Seeing the Emperor fall unconscious
at the very sight of the heir-apparent, the ladies of the royal household
start wailing piteously. On Sri Rama’s soliciting his permission to
retire to the woods, the king enjoins him to take his father
captive and ascend the throne. Sri Rama in his turn
consoles his father by assuring him that he has no
hankering for royal fortune and that to him
obedience to his father’s command is of
utmost importance. Dasaratha, however,
falls unconscious again at the very thought
of his separation from Sri Rama and
Sumantra as well as all the ladies of
the gynaeceum follow suit

Canto XXXVI

DaSaratha instructs Sumantra to take a detachment of the army and the
exchequer alongwith Sri Rama, to which Kaikeyi objects and insists
on his being sent into exile without any resources on the analogy

threatens to accompany the heir-apparent

Canto XL

Going clockwise round DaSaratha (as a token of respect), Sita, Rama and
Laksmana greet him. Accompanied by Sita, Sri Rama salutes Kausalya.
Laksmana too hails Kausalya first and then his own mother, Sumitra.
Sumitra for her part tenders salutary advice to her son. The princes
and the princess having mounted the chariot, Sumantra flicks
the horses. The citizens that had assembled, closely follow
the chariot; but unable to keep pace with its swift
movement, they return desolate. Dasaratha too
runs after the chariot alongwith Kausalya
and others, but being unable to walk
begins to totter and stops short
on the road yielding to the
remonstrances of his
wise ministers

Canto XLII

Sri Rama having departed for the forest in an exceptionally swift-going
chariot, Dasaratha vainly seeks to cover the intervening distance on foot.
The very dust raised by the chariot having disappeared after a while,
the Emperor feels doubly disconsolate and drops to the ground.
When Kaikeyi comes forward to support him, he scolds her and
asks her not to touch his person. Kausalya then lifts him up
and persuades him to return. His personal attendants
take him to the latter's apartments and, seeing him
plunged in grief, Kausalya seats herself beside
him and begins to lament in various ways

Canto XLVI

Having reached the bank of the Tamasa and thinking of the plight of the
people of Ayodhya, Sri Rama lays himself down on a bed of leaves
bewailing the lot of his parents and feeling reassured by the thought
of Bharata’s noble qualities; while Laksmana opens his dialogue
with Sumantra on the divine excellences of Sri Rama. Waking
up in the meantime, Sri Rama urges the charioteer-minister to
drive the chariot in such a way as to put the citizens, that
had accompanied them, off the scent and lead them to
think that the chariot had turned back towards
Ayodhya instead of proceeding towards the forest.

He then mounts the chariot alongwith Sita and
Laksmana and presses on to the forest
